about: Every recorded line in the games. The name on the left is the sound file; the words on the right are what the voice says. To change a line: edit the words, delete its sound file, and run tools/make-voice.py again. Only missing files are recorded, so nothing is paid for twice. A character whose voice id below is empty has not been given a voice yet, and their lines wait.

audio/g2/lesson/42-take-away-what-leaves: 42 take away what leaves 25? Count up from 25 to 42. The jumps tell us.
audio/g2/lesson/i-brought-my-coins-from-: I brought my coins from home in Canada! A nickel is 5 cents. A dime is 10 cents. A quarter is 25 cents.
audio/g2/lesson/start-with-the-biggest-c: Start with the biggest coin. 10 cents.
audio/g2/lesson/biggest-coins-first-then: Biggest coins first, then count on. That makes counting money easier!
audio/g2/lesson/start-with-the-biggest-c: Start with the biggest coin. 25 cents.
Start with the biggest coin. 2 dollars.
audio/g2/lesson/count-on-25-that-s-3-dol: Count on 25. That's 3 dollars and 25 cents.
audio/g2/lesson/count-on-10-that-s-3-dol: Count on 10. That's 3 dollars and 35 cents.
audio/g2/lesson/a-fig-costs-65-cents-and: A fig costs 65 cents and you pay with a loonie, 1 dollar. To find your change, count up from 65 cents to 1 dollar.
audio/g2/lesson/from-65-cents-to-70-cent: From 65 cents to 70 cents is 5 cents.
audio/g2/lesson/from-70-cents-to-1-dolla: From 70 cents to 1 dollar is 30 cents.
audio/g2/lesson/long-ago-people-in-egypt: Long ago, people in Egypt told the time with the sun. Let's think about how long things take!
audio/g2/lesson/we-measure-how-long-thin: We measure how long things take in seconds, minutes and hours.
audio/g2/lesson/a-second-is-very-short-i: A second is very short. It's about as quick as one clap.
audio/g2/lesson/a-minute-is-60-seconds-t: A minute is 60 seconds. That's about as long as counting slowly to 60.
audio/g2/lesson/an-hour-is-60-minutes-th: An hour is 60 minutes. That's much longer. Baking a loaf of bread takes about an hour.
audio/g2/lesson/a-boat-left-at-2-o-clock: A boat left at 2 o'clock and got to the next town at 5 o'clock. How long was the trip? Let's count the hours.
audio/g2/lesson/5-o-clock-is-3-hours-the: 5 o'clock is 3 hours. The trip took 3 hours!
audio/g2/lesson/opposites-are-words-that: Opposites are words that are as different as can be. Hot and cold are opposites.
audio/g2/lesson/try-them-in-sentences-th: Try them in sentences. The sand is hot. The snow is cold.
audio/g2/lesson/some-words-mean-the-same: Some words mean the same thing. Big and large mean the same.
audio/g2/lesson/swap-one-for-the-other-i: Swap one for the other in a sentence. A big pyramid. A large pyramid. It still means the same thing!
audio/g2/lesson/a-naming-word-called-a-n: A naming word, called a noun, names a person, a place or a thing. Here's a test: can you put 'the' in front of it? The pyramid. Yes! It's a noun.
audio/g2/lesson/an-action-word-called-a-: An action word, called a verb, is something you do. Test it: can you say 'I can' in front of it? I can dig. Yes! It's a verb.
audio/g2/lesson/a-describing-word-called: A describing word, called an adjective, tells us what something is like. A golden crown. Golden tells us what the crown is like.
audio/g2/lesson/a-scribe-had-to-spell-ev: A scribe had to spell every word the right way. Let's try!
audio/g2/lesson/some-sounds-are-spelled-: Some sounds are spelled with a team of letters. In rain, the A and the I work together to make the long A sound. In boat, O A makes the long O sound. In night, I G H makes the long I sound.
audio/g2/lesson/and-in-cake-the-e-at-the: And in cake, the E at the end is silent. It makes the A say its name.
audio/g2/lesson/some-words-have-a-tricky: Some words have a tricky part that doesn't sound the way it looks. We call them heart words, because we learn the tricky part by heart.
audio/g2/lesson/in-friend-the-tricky-par: In friend, the tricky part is I E. Look at it, say the letters, and remember it: F, R, I, E, N, D.
audio/g2/lesson/to-mean-more-than-one-mo: To mean more than one, most words just add S. One cat, two cats.
audio/g2/lesson/words-that-end-in-s-x-s-: Words that end in S, X, S H or C H add E S. One box, two boxes.
audio/g2/lesson/if-a-word-ends-in-a-cons: If a word ends in a consonant and Y, change the Y to I and add E S. One baby, two babies.
audio/g2/lesson/and-some-words-change-co: And some words change completely. One mouse, two mice!
audio/g2/lesson/to-talk-about-yesterday-: To talk about yesterday, most words add E D. Today I jump. Yesterday I jumped.
audio/g2/lesson/short-words-like-stop-do: Short words like stop double the last letter first. Stopped.
audio/g2/lesson/and-some-words-change-co: And some words change completely. Today I go. Yesterday I went. Say it in a sentence to hear which one sounds right.
audio/g2/lesson/let-s-read-about-egypt-l: Let's read about Egypt, long ago and today!
audio/g2/lesson/here-s-how-good-readers-: Here's how good readers find answers. First, read the question. Why were cats helpful?
audio/g2/lesson/then-look-in-the-scroll-: Then look in the scroll for the sentence that answers it. Cats kept mice away from the food.
audio/g2/lesson/so-cats-were-helpful-bec: So cats were helpful because they kept mice away. The answer was right there in the scroll!
audio/g2/lesson/the-pyramids-were-built-: The pyramids were built from rows and rows of stones. Let's count them the quick way!
audio/g2/lesson/here-are-3-rows-of-4-sto: Here are 3 rows of 4 stones. Counting them one at a time is slow. Let's count by fours instead!
audio/g2/lesson/that-s-the-same-as-4-plu: That's the same as 4 plus 4 plus 4.

audio/g4/lesson/every-night-the-legion-b: Every night, the legion built a camp laid out on a neat grid. Let's find things on the map!
audio/g4/lesson/watch-me-find-the-tent-o: Watch me find the tent on the map. The map is cut into squares. Letters go along the bottom, and numbers go up the side.
audio/g4/lesson/first-i-find-the-letter-: First I find the letter. The tent is above the letter C.
audio/g4/lesson/then-i-find-the-number-b: Then I find the number beside it. The tent is in row 4.
audio/g4/lesson/so-the-tent-is-in-square: So the tent is in square C4! The letter comes first, then the number.
audio/g4/lesson/watch-me-read-coordinate: Watch me read coordinates. The shield sits where two lines cross.
audio/g4/lesson/i-start-at-zero-first-i-: I start at zero. First I go along the bottom, 3 lines across. Along the corridor.
audio/g4/lesson/then-i-go-up-5-lines-up-: Then I go up 5 lines. Up the stairs!
audio/g4/lesson/so-the-shield-is-at-3-5-: So the shield is at 3, 5. Across first, then up.
audio/g4/lesson/watch-me-move-the-legion: Watch me move the legion. It starts at 1, 2. The order is: march 4 right, and 3 up.
audio/g4/lesson/that-move-is-called-a-sl: That move is called a slide. The legion slid to 5, 5, and it still faces the same way.
audio/g4/lesson/watch-me-flip-the-shield: Watch me flip the shield across the river. It's a mirror image, like looking in water.
audio/g4/lesson/the-shield-is-3-squares-: The shield is 3 squares to the left of the river.
audio/g4/lesson/its-mirror-image-is-the-: Its mirror image is the same distance on the other side. 3 squares to the right.
audio/g4/lesson/it-stays-at-the-same-hei: It stays at the same height. So the flipped shield lands at 7, 3!
audio/g4/lesson/roman-soldiers-marched-i: Roman soldiers marched in neat formations, and their patterns help us predict what comes next!
audio/g4/lesson/watch-me-with-a-mosaic-p: Watch me with a mosaic pattern. First, I find the part that repeats.
audio/g4/lesson/red-gold-gold-then-it-st: Red, gold, gold. Then it starts again.
audio/g4/lesson/after-red-comes-gold-so-: After red comes gold. So the next tile is gold!
audio/g4/lesson/watch-me-with-a-growing-: Watch me with a growing pattern. Formation 1 has 2 soldiers. Formation 2 has 4. Formation 3 has 6.
audio/g4/lesson/each-time-2-more-soldier: Each time, 2 more soldiers join. That's the pattern rule: add 2.
audio/g4/lesson/watch-me-with-a-shrinkin: Watch me with a shrinking pattern. The grain store starts with 50 sacks. Each day, the legion eats 5.
audio/g4/lesson/the-rule-is-take-away-5-: The rule is: take away 5 each day.
audio/g4/lesson/here-s-a-shortcut-after-: Here's a shortcut. After 3 days, they've eaten 3 times 5, which is 15. 50 take away 15 is 35. It matches the table!
audio/g4/lesson/watch-me-compare-legion-: Watch me compare. Legion A has 3 rows of 8 soldiers. Legion B has 25 soldiers.
audio/g4/lesson/first-i-work-out-each-si: First I work out each side. 3 times 8 is 24.
audio/g4/lesson/24-is-less-than-25-the-s: 24 is less than 25. The small pointy end of the sign points to the smaller number. So 3 times 8 is less than 25!
audio/g4/lesson/a-picture-graph-has-a-ke: A picture graph has a key. Here, each shield stands for 10 soldiers. Two and a half shields is 25 soldiers!
audio/g4/lesson/watch-me-read-a-double-b: Watch me read a double bar graph. It shows two legions side by side. Blue is the Third Legion. Red is the Ninth Legion.
audio/g4/lesson/at-running-the-blue-bar-: At running, the blue bar reaches 30, and the red bar reaches 70. The Ninth Legion scored more!
audio/g4/lesson/a-bag-can-show-how-likel: A bag can show how likely something is. 6 tokens are red, and only 2 are gold. Picking gold is unlikely. Picking red is likely!

audio/g5/intro/out-with-the-old-in-with-: Out with the old, in with the new! It's been a hoooot!
audio/g5/intro/but-there-is-one-place-i-: But there is one place I have never properly explored. I flew right over it every time, on my way to somewhere else.
audio/g5/intro/home-canada-it-turns-out-: Home. Canada. It turns out the biggest adventure was waiting right where I started.
audio/g5/intro/i-have-seen-pyramids-i-ha: I have seen pyramids. I have walked the Great Wall. I have counted every arch in Rome. Twice.
audio/g5/intro/my-lunch-so-that-s-which-: My lunch! So that's which century I left it in. It has not aged well.
audio/g5/intro/new-goggles-new-scarf-sam: New goggles. New scarf. Same owl. And for the first time in a very long while, I know exactly where I'm going.
audio/g5/intro/well-are-you-coming-tick-: Well? Are you coming? Tick tock!
audio/g5/s/a-long-journey-to-a-new-home-: A long journey to a new home. Three right answers and we look at the land.
audio/g5/s/a-winter-journey-three-right-: A winter journey. Three right answers and we get to summer.
audio/g5/s/after-the-american-revolution: After the American Revolution, a war just to the south, these families had lost their homes. Joseph Brant led them here, to the Grand River, to begin again.
audio/g5/s/all-the-way-north-this-is-ee-: All the way north! This is Ee-ka-loo-eet, in Nunavut. I am wearing every scarf I own, all at once.
audio/g5/s/and-look-up-the-northern-ligh: And look up. The northern lights! First things first, though. Just how cold is it out there?
audio/g5/s/and-people-still-paddle-these: And people still paddle these routes. Some canoes are made of new materials now. Some are still made of birchbark, the old way.
audio/g5/s/and-there-is-lily-waving-she-: And there is Lily, waving! She says there is one more story, and it belongs to this very spot.
audio/g5/s/before-i-go-some-mail-has-arr: Before I go, some mail has arrived. Four letters! From Lily, Noah, Maya and Nina.
audio/g5/s/corn-beans-and-squash-grow-to: Corn, beans and squash grow together on little hills of earth. The corn is a pole for the beans to climb.
audio/g5/s/corn-hangs-from-the-roof-to-d: Corn hangs from the roof to dry. Lily wonders how many people lived in here. Hmm. I'll need my multiplying goggles.
audio/g5/s/count-the-geese-with-us-three: Count the geese with us. Three right answers and Maya has something to teach me.
audio/g5/s/each-of-them-has-sent-me-one-: Each of them has sent me one last question, to see if I was paying attention.
audio/g5/s/families-camped-together-by-t: Families camped together by the water for the goose hunt. Maya's grandfather still counts the geese each spring. Let's count with him.
audio/g5/s/fires-burn-in-a-row-down-the-: Fires burn in a row down the middle. Each fire is shared by two families, one on each side.
audio/g5/s/help-build-the-ig-loo-three-r: Help build the ig-loo. Three right answers and we go travelling.
audio/g5/s/help-me-load-the-canoe-three-: Help me load the canoe. Three right answers and we set off.
audio/g5/s/help-me-measure-the-longhouse: Help me measure the longhouses. Three right answers opens the door!
audio/g5/s/help-me-with-the-calendar-thr: Help me with the calendar. Three right answers and the window shows us winter.
audio/g5/s/here-is-how-you-cut-blocks-of: Here is how. You cut blocks of hard snow and stand them in a ring. Then you build round and round in a spiral, leaning in a little each time.
audio/g5/s/history-is-not-only-long-ago-: History is not only long ago. Some of it is still happening. Now then. How old is that chapel?
audio/g5/s/home-at-last-i-started-this-t: Home at last. I started this trip right here in southern Ontario, and I have come all the way around.
audio/g5/s/how-cold-is-it-three-right-an: How cold is it? Three right answers and Nina shows us how to build a snow house.
audio/g5/s/how-far-is-the-trip-three-rig: How far is the trip? Three right answers and we get a closer look at the canoe.
audio/g5/s/how-long-ago-was-it-three-rig: How long ago was it? Three right answers finishes the chapter.
audio/g5/s/how-long-is-the-day-three-rig: How long is the day? Three right answers finishes the chapter.
audio/g5/s/how-long-will-it-take-three-r: How long will it take? Three right answers and the window shows us one more thing.
audio/g5/s/how-many-people-lived-in-a-lo: How many people lived in a longhouse? Three right answers and we step back outside.
audio/g5/s/i-asked-nina-how-anyone-could: I asked Nina how anyone could live where it is this cold. She said, very cleverly. Clock, show us!
audio/g5/s/i-did-it-with-a-great-deal-of: I did it! With a great deal of help from you.
audio/g5/s/i-have-been-all-the-way-to-th: I have been all the way to the top of my country. There is only one place left to go. Home. Tick tock!
audio/g5/s/i-said-there-are-four-seasons: I said there are four seasons. Maya says, count again.
audio/g5/s/i-told-maya-i-had-learned-to-: I told Maya I had learned to say mee-gwetch. She laughed. In her language, thank you is mee-gwetch, and you say it the same way, mee-gwetch. Almost the same word! Their languages are cousins.
audio/g5/s/i-tried-to-count-them-i-got-t: I tried to count them. I got to forty and lost my place. Lily's friend lives near here. He has promised to show me the best way to travel. I hope it's a balloon.
audio/g5/s/i-was-mostly-you-had-better-h: I was. Mostly. You had better help me.
audio/g5/s/i-went-looking-for-my-country: I went looking for my country, and I found the peoples who have always been here. Ho-dee-no-show-nee, Ah-nish-ih-nah-bay, Cree and Ih-noo-it. Still here. Still teaching.
audio/g5/s/in-the-middle-of-winter-here-: In the middle of winter here, the sun only comes up for a few hours. The rest is night. So how did people find their way?
audio/g5/s/in-those-two-seasons-you-can-: In those two seasons you can't paddle the river, and you can't walk on it either. You wait. So you had better know your calendar!
audio/g5/s/in-winter-families-spread-out: In winter, families spread out across the land, so there was enough food for everyone. They walked on snowshoes, which stop you sinking into the snow.
audio/g5/s/it-is-named-for-joseph-brant-: It is named for Joseph Brant. He was a Mohawk leader, and his Mohawk name was Tie-en-da-nay-gee-uh. You say it tie-en-da-nay-gee-uh.
audio/g5/s/it-is-not-a-balloon-it-s-a-ca: It is not a balloon. It's a canoe! This is Noah. His family is Ah-nish-ih-nah-bay. You say it ah-nish-ih-nah-bay.
audio/g5/s/it-is-strong-enough-to-carry-: It is strong enough to carry a family and everything they own, and light enough for two people to lift. Why would you lift a boat? You'll see. First, let's load it up.
audio/g5/s/it-s-called-goose-break-every: It's called goose break. Every spring, schools here take a holiday so families can go out on the land together, just as they always have.
audio/g5/s/let-s-count-the-garden-three-: Let's count the garden. Three right answers and the window closes.
audio/g5/s/let-s-weigh-the-harvest-three: Let's weigh the harvest. Three right answers finishes the chapter.
audio/g5/s/lily-says-her-own-people-the-: Lily says her own people, the Ho-dee-no-show-nee, lived in longhouse villages just like this one, around the lake to the south.
audio/g5/s/lily-says-it-means-people-of-: Lily says it means People of the Longhouse. Her people have lived around these lakes for a very, very long time.
audio/g5/s/lily-says-the-story-did-not-e: Lily says the story did not end there. Over the years, most of that promised land was taken or sold off without their agreement, and people are still working to put that right today.
audio/g5/s/look-closely-no-nails-no-meta: Look closely. No nails. No metal at all.
audio/g5/s/many-cree-families-count-six-: Many Cree families count six. Between winter and spring comes break-up, when the river ice cracks and floats away. Between fall and winter comes freeze-up.
audio/g5/s/maya-said-somebody-here-could: Maya said somebody here could teach me how to live in the cold. I hope so. My beak has frozen shut twice.
audio/g5/s/maya-says-i-have-come-at-the-: Maya says I have come at the best time of year. It is spring, and the geese are coming back. Clock, show us what that meant long ago!
audio/g5/s/maya-says-if-i-liked-the-snow: Maya says if I liked the snow, I should keep going north. All the way north. That is another chapter. Tick tock!
audio/g5/s/measure-the-land-along-the-ri: Measure the land along the river. Three right answers and Lily shows us something very old.
audio/g5/s/mee-gwetch-maya-i-counted-six: Mee-gwetch, Maya. I counted six seasons, one thousand geese and four mosquitoes. The mosquitoes found me first.
audio/g5/s/my-balloon-can-t-fly-through-: My balloon can't fly through time any more. But look what its clock can do now. A window into the past!
audio/g5/s/na-koor-meek-nina-i-have-lear: Na-koor-meek, Nina. I have learned that snow can be warm, that stones can give directions, and that I need a much bigger scarf.
audio/g5/s/next-lily-says-we-should-foll: Next, Lily says we should follow the water north, by canoe. But that is another chapter. Tick tock!
audio/g5/s/nina-s-grandfather-still-driv: Nina's grandfather still drives a dog team. He says the dogs know the way home better than he does. Let's pack the sled.
audio/g5/s/nina-s-word-for-a-house-is-ig: Nina's word for a house is ig-loo. You say it ig-loo. A snow ig-loo kept a family warm on winter journeys, even when the wind outside was fierce.
audio/g5/s/nina-s-word-for-thank-you-is-: Nina's word for thank you is na-koor-meek. You say it na-koor-meek. That is four languages I can say thank you in now. Five, with hoot.
audio/g5/s/nina-says-it-can-be-freezing-: Nina says it can be freezing outside and warm enough inside to take your coat off. Snow, keeping you warm! Let's count the blocks.
audio/g5/s/noah-has-done-this-he-says-th: Noah has done this. He says the canoe is fine. It's the mosquitoes that are heavy.
audio/g5/s/noah-paddles-every-summer-wit: Noah paddles every summer with his uncle. He says the lakes and rivers were the highways here, long before there were any roads. Clock, show us!
audio/g5/s/noah-said-the-seasons-decide-: Noah said the seasons decide everything here. I packed for four seasons. I am told that is not enough.
audio/g5/s/noah-says-if-i-think-this-is-: Noah says if I think this is far, I should try going north, where the seasons decide everything. That is another chapter. Tick tock!
audio/g5/s/noah-says-one-trading-trip-co: Noah says one trading trip could be hundreds of kilometres. Let's work out how far these paddlers are going.
audio/g5/s/north-again-the-roads-ran-out: North again! The roads ran out a long time ago. Up here it is rivers, spruce trees and sky.
audio/g5/s/nunavut-means-our-land-it-bec: Nunavut means our land. It became Canada's newest territory in 1999. Nina's grandmother remembers the day.
audio/g5/s/nyah-wen-mee-gwetch-mee-gwetc: Nyah-wen. Mee-gwetch. Mee-gwetch. Na-koor-meek. And thank you.
audio/g5/s/one-more-thing-before-we-go-i: One more thing before we go. I want to know how long ago that village was. Help me with the years.
audio/g5/s/one-of-the-first-things-they-: One of the first things they built was this little chapel, in 1785. It is still standing! It is the oldest church still standing in Ontario.
audio/g5/s/one-question-from-each-friend: One question from each friend. Four right answers finishes the story!
audio/g5/s/one-star-hardly-moves-at-all-: One star hardly moves at all, and the others slowly turn around it, like the hands of my clock. I like that star.
audio/g5/s/outside-the-village-are-the-g: Outside the village are the gardens. Lily's grandmother still plants hers this way. It's called the Three Sisters.
audio/g5/s/pack-the-sled-three-right-ans: Pack the sled. Three right answers and night falls.
audio/g5/s/read-the-stars-three-right-an: Read the stars. Three right answers finishes the chapter.
audio/g5/s/see-the-pile-of-stones-on-the: See the pile of stones on the hill? That is an ih-nook-sook. You say it ih-nook-sook. People built them to mark the way, so that travellers would not get lost.
audio/g5/s/six-nations-settled-here-toge: Six nations settled here together. The Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, Seneca and Tuscarora.
audio/g5/s/some-grains-always-fall-back-: Some grains always fall back into the water. That's on purpose. They grow into next year's rice.
audio/g5/s/somebody-is-waiting-to-show-m: Somebody is waiting to show me around. I do hope they like owls.
audio/g5/s/summer-the-opposite-of-winter: Summer! The opposite of winter in every way. Families who were far apart all winter came back together by the river.
audio/g5/s/tall-grass-growing-right-out-: Tall grass, growing right out of the water, in a shallow, sheltered bay! Noah says it is wild rice. In his language it's mah-noo-min. You say it mah-noo-min.
audio/g5/s/thank-you-lily-nyah-wen-you-s: Thank you, Lily. Nyah-wen. You say it nyah-wen. That means thank you in Mohawk, Lily's language. I practised.
audio/g5/s/thank-you-noah-mee-gwetch-you: Thank you, Noah. Mee-gwetch. You say it mee-gwetch. That's thank you in his language. My arms feel like jelly.
audio/g5/s/that-is-why-lily-s-community-: That is why Lily's community is called Six Nations of the Grand River. Let's see how much land that promise was.
audio/g5/s/that-river-below-is-the-grand: That river below is the Grand River. It winds for about 280 kilometres, all the way down to Lake Erie.
audio/g5/s/the-ah-nish-ih-nah-bay-are-ma: The Ah-nish-ih-nah-bay are many peoples, like the Ojibwe, the Odawa and the Potawatomi. They have lived around the Great Lakes for thousands of years.
audio/g5/s/the-beans-feed-the-soil-the-b: The beans feed the soil. The big squash leaves shade the ground and keep the weeds away. Three plants helping each other!
audio/g5/s/the-clock-is-ticking-again-an: The clock is ticking again, and it is pointing east. There is a lot more of Canada to see. But that is another grade. Tick tock!
audio/g5/s/the-families-were-promised-la: The families were promised land of their own: along the Grand River, from its mouth to where it begins, and about 10 kilometres back from the water on each side.
audio/g5/s/the-frame-is-cedar-wood-the-s: The frame is cedar wood. The skin is bark from birch trees, sewn together with spruce roots. Sticky spruce gum seals it to keep the water out.
audio/g5/s/the-last-block-fits-in-the-to: The last block fits in the top, like a lid. Inside, a stone lamp called a koo-lik burns oil for light and heat. You say it koo-lik.
audio/g5/s/the-longhouse-is-still-here-t: The longhouse is still here too. Not for sleeping in. It is where the community gathers for traditional ceremonies and big decisions.
audio/g5/s/the-longhouses-are-made-of-wo: The longhouses are made of wooden poles covered in sheets of bark. Lily wants to know how big one is. Good question. Let's measure.
audio/g5/s/the-mohawk-are-one-of-the-ho-: The Mohawk are one of the Ho-dee-no-show-nee nations, like Lily's family. Clock, one last window, please!
audio/g5/s/the-window-into-the-past-a-wi: The window into the past! A winter camp, long ago. Those round houses are made of snow.
audio/g5/s/the-window-into-the-past-it-i: The window into the past! It is spring there too, hundreds of years ago. Look at the sky!
audio/g5/s/the-window-into-the-past-the-: The window into the past! The very same bay, hundreds of years ago. And it is busy.
audio/g5/s/the-window-is-closed-and-here: The window is closed, and here we are, today. And look. The same three plants, in Lily's grandmother's garden.
audio/g5/s/the-window-is-closed-but-noah: The window is closed. But Noah says his family still harvests mah-noo-min, every year at the end of summer.
audio/g5/s/the-window-is-closed-it-is-sp: The window is closed. It is spring again, today. And Maya's school is closed too!
audio/g5/s/the-window-is-closed-this-is-: The window is closed. This is Nina's town, today. Bright houses, a school, and snowmobiles parked beside the sleds.
audio/g5/s/the-year-is-1784-not-so-very-: The year is 1784. Not so very long ago, this time. And look how many people!
audio/g5/s/there-are-no-trees-here-at-al: There are no trees here at all. Just rock, snow, sea ice, and the biggest sky I have ever seen.
audio/g5/s/they-crossed-the-river-at-a-s: They crossed the river at a shallow place. People called it Brant's ford. Say it quickly. Brant's ford. Brantford!
audio/g5/s/they-fished-picked-berries-to: They fished, picked berries, told stories and visited. And the sun hardly went to bed at all.
audio/g5/s/they-pulled-their-things-on-a: They pulled their things on a toboggan. Peoples of the north invented both, and we still use them today. Let's go for a walk. A long one.
audio/g5/s/they-read-the-land-and-the-sk: They read the land and the sky. The shapes the wind carves in the snow. The ih-nook-sook on the hill. And the stars.
audio/g5/s/they-still-do-lily-goes-to-sc: They still do! Lily goes to school, plays lacrosse, and helps in her grandmother's garden. I asked what a longhouse is. She said, look for yourself.
audio/g5/s/this-far-north-summer-days-ar: This far north, summer days are very long and winter days are very short. I would like to know exactly how long.
audio/g5/s/this-is-maya-her-family-is-cr: This is Maya. Her family is Cree. They have lived on this land for thousands of years.
audio/g5/s/this-is-my-new-friend-lily-he: This is my new friend Lily. Her family is Ho-dee-no-show-nee. You say it ho-dee-no-show-nee.
audio/g5/s/this-is-nina-she-is-an-ih-noo: This is Nina. She is an Ih-nook. You say it ih-nook. Her people are the Ih-noo-it, ih-noo-it, which means the people. They have lived in the Arctic for thousands of years.
audio/g5/s/this-is-the-land-at-the-south: This is the land at the south end of James Bay, near Moose Factory, at the very top of Ontario. It is so flat and wet that the ground wobbled when I landed. People call it muskeg.
audio/g5/s/this-is-the-very-same-spot-ab: This is the very same spot, about 600 years ago. A whole village! Those long buildings are the longhouses. The people living here then were the At-ta-wan-da-ron, cousins of the Ho-dee-no-show-nee.
audio/g5/s/this-is-why-when-the-river-ge: This is why! When the river gets too rough, or the lake ends, you carry your canoe over land to the next water. It's called a portage.
audio/g5/s/this-part-is-called-georgian-: This part is called Georgian Bay. Rock, pine trees, and islands everywhere. People call it the Thirty Thousand Islands.
audio/g5/s/this-town-is-called-brantford: This town is called Brantford. Lily asked if I knew where the name came from. I guessed a man named Ford. I was half right.
audio/g5/s/those-are-birchbark-canoes-pe: Those are birchbark canoes. People are carrying food, tools and furs to trade with other nations, far across the lakes.
audio/g5/s/thousands-and-thousands-of-ge: Thousands and thousands of geese, flying north. After a long winter, this meant fresh food for everyone.
audio/g5/s/to-travel-families-used-a-lon: To travel, families used a long sled called a kah-moo-teek, pulled by a team of dogs. You say it kah-moo-teek.
audio/g5/s/we-can-look-inside-one-longho: We can look inside! One longhouse was home to many families, all related through their mothers and grandmothers.
audio/g5/s/we-followed-the-water-north-j: We followed the water north, just as Lily said. And look at that. Lake Huron! It goes on forever.
audio/g5/s/what-a-day-i-thought-i-knew-m: What a day. I thought I knew my own country. I had hardly looked!
audio/g5/s/where-to-begin-right-here-i-t: Where to begin? Right here, I think. Southern Ontario, where the balloon came down.
audio/g5/s/winter-deep-snow-and-the-rive: Winter. Deep snow, and the river frozen as hard as a road.
audio/g5/s/with-all-this-paddling-and-ca: With all this paddling and carrying, how long does a trip take? I'll need my thinking goggles.
audio/g5/s/work-out-the-years-three-righ: Work out the years. Three right answers and the mail arrives.
audio/g5/s/you-paddle-slowly-through-it-: You paddle slowly through it, and gently knock the ripe grains into the canoe with two sticks.
audio/g6/s/a-farm-is-la-ferme-like-most-: A farm is la ferme. Like most farms around here, his is long and thin. Not a square in sight.
audio/g6/s/a-field-is-le-champ-where-the: A field is le champ. Where the river bends, some fields get cut on a slant, which makes them tricky to measure. Shall we try?
audio/g6/s/a-girl-is-waving-from-the-sho: A girl is waving from the shore. This is Sadie. She is a Meeg-maw girl (you say it meeg-maw), and she lives in a community right beside the lake.
audio/g6/s/a-horse-pulls-us-through-the-: A horse pulls us through the maple wood. The snow squeaks, and the sap buckets slide by on the trees.
audio/g6/s/a-little-tour-boat-takes-us-o: A little tour boat takes us out through the narrow harbour entrance, between the cliffs. And there it is, a white and blue mountain floating in the sea. I feel extremely small.
audio/g6/s/a-maple-tree-is-l-rable-it-ta: A maple tree is l'érable. It takes about 40 litres of sap to make just 1 litre of syrup. That is a lot of buckets and a lot of boiling.
audio/g6/s/a-sign-on-the-dock-says-bienv: A sign on the dock says bienvenue, which is French for welcome. I waved at the sign. It did not wave back, but it was very polite.
audio/g6/s/a-sleigh-is-le-tra-neau-the-h: A sleigh is le traîneau. The horse stayed calm the whole ride. I did not, but I am an owl, and owls are dramatic.
audio/g6/s/about-3-000-of-them-are-black: About 3,000 of them are Black Loyalists. They are people of African descent who were promised freedom and land if they sided with Britain. Many cross by boat, le bateau in French.
audio/g6/s/after-europeans-settled-the-c: After Europeans settled the coasts, the Bee-oth-uk were cut off from the sea they fished. There was fighting with settlers, and new sicknesses came. Their numbers fell and fell.
audio/g6/s/all-aboard-the-ferry-crosses-: All aboard! The ferry crosses to Dartmouth, on the other side of the harbour. It is the oldest saltwater ferry service in North America, and it has been running since 1752.
audio/g6/s/amara-has-two-ideas-for-the-a: Amara has two ideas for the afternoon. We could ride the harbour ferry across the water, or climb the hill again to hear the noon gun. Which shall we do?
audio/g6/s/amara-is-buying-ferry-tickets: Amara is buying ferry tickets for the ride home. Three right answers and we say goodbye.
audio/g6/s/amara-says-a-ferry-is-le-trav: Amara says a ferry is le traversier. The wind is fresh and the gulls follow us. I held on tight to my feathers.
audio/g6/s/and-all-this-land-is-meeg-mah: And all this land is Meeg-mah-gee, the Meeg-maw homeland. You say it meeg-mah-gee. It covers the Maritime provinces and more.
audio/g6/s/and-here-is-the-best-part-tho: And here is the best part. Those treaties are still in force today, and every October 1 is Treaty Day in Nova Scotia. They still protect Meeg-maw rights today, such as fishing and gathering.
audio/g6/s/au-revoir-lodie-east-we-go-ag: Au revoir, Élodie! East we go again. Tick tock!
audio/g6/s/back-on-the-shore-sadie-has-d: Back on the shore, Sadie has drawn a star in the sand. Time to talk about turns!
audio/g6/s/back-to-the-window-and-now-it: Back to the window, and now it is the 1500s. The harbour is full of ships! Fishing crews cross the ocean from Europe every summer.
Back to the window, and now it is the 1700s. Meeg-maw leaders and British officials stand at a table with a paper between them. This is a treaty, a promise made between two peoples.
audio/g6/s/back-to-the-window-the-dock-i: Back to the window. The dock is busy again! The long, low building is Pier 21, and an ocean liner is tied up beside it.
audio/g6/s/back-to-the-window-the-riverb: Back to the window. The riverbank is busy! People are trading.
audio/g6/s/back-to-today-from-up-here-th: Back to today! From up here the fields still look like ribbons. Some are strawberries, some are hay, and some are just having a nap.
audio/g6/s/back-to-today-look-at-the-boa: Back to today. Look at the boats! They are sitting on the mud, and the sea has gone far away. Did somebody pull the plug?
audio/g6/s/black-nova-scotians-have-been: Black Nova Scotians have been part of this province for well over 200 years, and they are here today. Harbour clerks had to count everyone who came ashore, so let's count too.
audio/g6/s/boats-carried-people-and-good: Boats carried people and goods, and in winter the frozen river was a road too. So the houses stood close together along the shore, and neighbours could wave. Let's measure these lots.
audio/g6/s/boots-on-at-low-tide-the-sea-: Boots on! At low tide the sea floor is red-brown mud, and every step goes squish. Élodie says we must stay close to shore, because the tide comes back fast.
audio/g6/s/but-look-at-lodie-s-flag-acad: But look at Élodie's flag! Acadians are still here, still speaking French, with a flag of blue, white and red and a gold star. A flag is le drapeau.
audio/g6/s/but-that-is-another-story-tic: But that is another story. Tick tock!
audio/g6/s/but-this-island-was-not-empty: But this island was not empty. The Bee-oth-uk lived across it for a very long time. You say it bee-oth-uk.
audio/g6/s/canada-has-two-official-langu: Canada has two official languages, English and French. So I am practising my French all the way to the coast.
audio/g6/s/cape-spear-this-is-the-very-e: Cape Spear! This is the very edge of the map. It is the most easterly point in North America, and the sun rises here first. There is no more east to go.
audio/g6/s/champlain-s-ship-took-about-t: Champlain's ship took about two months to cross the ocean. Two months! I get restless in the bath. Let's work out that journey.
audio/g6/s/check-the-clocks-with-declan-: Check the clocks with Declan. Three right answers and we go to see some ice.
audio/g6/s/check-the-poles-and-the-star-: Check the poles and the star corners with Sadie. Three right answers and the window opens again.
audio/g6/s/count-down-to-the-noon-gun-th: Count down to the noon gun. Three right answers and the window opens again.
audio/g6/s/count-the-beads-and-quills-wi: Count the beads and quills with Sadie. Three right answers and we pick our afternoon.
audio/g6/s/count-the-people-stepping-off: Count the people stepping off the ships. Three right answers and we climb the hill.
audio/g6/s/declan-has-two-ideas-for-the-: Declan has two ideas for the afternoon. Shall we take a boat out to see an iceberg up close, or walk the cliff to watch the puffins?
audio/g6/s/declan-says-newfoundland-has-: Declan says Newfoundland has its own time zone. The clocks here are half an hour ahead of the rest of Atlantic Canada. My balloon clock is very confused.
audio/g6/s/declan-says-the-norse-had-no-: Declan says the Norse had no watches. He has one, and it is half an hour ahead of Halifax. Let's work out the time.
audio/g6/s/do-the-iceberg-sums-with-decl: Do the iceberg sums with Declan. Three right answers and the window opens again.
audio/g6/s/do-the-syrup-sums-three-right: Do the syrup sums. Three right answers and we visit the sugar shack.
audio/g6/s/down-the-coast-we-float-and-t: Down the coast we float, and the clock has found a harbour. A big one! Ships are sliding in and out, and a red and white lighthouse is watching them go.
audio/g6/s/down-the-hill-stands-the-town: Down the hill stands the Town Clock, a white tower with a clock face on every side. As a clock inventor, I bowed to it. Now, how long until the gun goes off?
audio/g6/s/down-the-river-out-to-sea-and: Down the river, out to sea, and then south! The clock has brought us to the Bay of Fundy, where the tides are the biggest in the world.
audio/g6/s/each-lot-was-farmed-by-a-fami: Each lot was farmed by a family of habitants, which is what the French farmers were called. Every family got a piece of the riverbank, because the river was the road.
audio/g6/s/each-person-walked-through-th: Each person walked through the doors with a suitcase, which is la valise in French. Many then took a train and rode west across the country.
audio/g6/s/east-we-go-again-the-clock-fo: East we go again! The clock followed the coast, and now we float over an island with a great blue lake right in the middle. Hold on to your hat. I landed on a goose last time.
audio/g6/s/east-we-go-the-clock-pointed-: East we go! The clock pointed this way, and look what it found. A city on a cliff, with a castle on top.
audio/g6/s/every-day-at-twelve-o-clock-a: Every day at twelve o'clock, a cannon here goes BOOM. It is called the noon gun, and it is a Halifax tradition. Even the seagulls know to leave early.
audio/g6/s/every-good-trade-ends-with-a-: Every good trade ends with a thank you. In French, that is merci. Now then. How many furs for a kettle?
audio/g6/s/every-spring-something-enormo: Every spring, something enormous floats past this coast. Icebergs! They break off glaciers far to the north and drift south along Iceberg Alley.
audio/g6/s/families-fished-and-gathered-: Families fished and gathered by the sea in the warm months, and moved inland for winter. Many Meeg-maw families still fish and gather along these waters today.
audio/g6/s/family-in-french-is-la-famill: Family in French is la famille, and hers is a big one. Her grandmother, her cousins and a dog named Moustache all come for Sunday supper.
audio/g6/s/fifty-nine-steps-l-a-skipped-: Fifty-nine steps. Léa skipped up. I counted every one, out loud. In French, stairs are l'escalier.
audio/g6/s/first-nations-of-this-region-: First Nations of this region, among them the Abenaki, the Algonquin and the Wendat, made maple sugar long before any ships came. They taught the French settlers how.
audio/g6/s/first-nations-peoples-had-liv: First Nations peoples had lived along this river for thousands of years before he came. The name Quebec comes from an Algonquin word. It means where the river narrows.
audio/g6/s/first-nations-trappers-and-tr: First Nations trappers and traders were skilled partners. They knew the land, and they drove the trade. Later, the rush for beaver brought over-trapping, fighting, and new sicknesses that killed very many people.
audio/g6/s/from-1928-to-1971-about-one-m: From 1928 to 1971, about one million immigrants arrived in Canada through Pier 21. Families came from many countries, after days at sea.
audio/g6/s/goodbye-l-a-my-clock-balloon-: Goodbye, Léa! My clock balloon is drifting downriver, and the St. Lawrence is slowly getting wider.
audio/g6/s/he-greets-me-with-whaddaya-at: He greets me with Whaddaya at? That is a Newfoundland way to ask how you are doing. I said I was at being an owl. Declan laughed anyway.
audio/g6/s/he-says-quebec-makes-most-of-: He says Quebec makes most of the maple syrup in the whole world. I believe him. I have the sticky feathers to prove it.
audio/g6/s/help-build-the-dyke-three-rig: Help build the dyke. Three right answers and we meet the tides.
audio/g6/s/help-sadie-with-her-star-in-t: Help Sadie with her star in the sand. Three right answers and we go to see the star in her community.
audio/g6/s/help-the-clerk-with-his-tally: Help the clerk with his tally. Three right answers and we choose our own way.
audio/g6/s/hot-syrup-is-poured-in-lines-: Hot syrup is poured in lines on clean snow. It cools into chewy taffy, and you roll it up onto a stick. Olivier says it is the best part of spring.
audio/g6/s/i-know-one-french-word-bonjou: I know one French word. Bonjour! It means hello. I have said it to nine people and a pigeon.
audio/g6/s/in-french-a-harbour-is-le-por: In French, a harbour is le port. Amara says every family here has a story about arriving, and some of the oldest ones can be seen through the clock. Clock, show us!
audio/g6/s/in-french-a-puffin-is-le-maca: In French a puffin is le macareux. Declan says it looks like it is wearing a clown's nose. I say it is the best beak I have ever seen.
audio/g6/s/in-french-it-is-l-iceberg-the: In French it is l'iceberg. The very same word! That is one French word I did not have to practise.
audio/g6/s/in-french-it-is-la-tire-mine-: In French it is la tire. Mine stuck to my feathers. I may be sticky until Tuesday.
audio/g6/s/in-french-noon-is-midi-which-: In French, noon is midi, which really means the middle of the day. Down below, the Town Clock looked very pleased with itself.
audio/g6/s/in-french-the-island-is-calle: In French the island is called Terre-Neuve. That means new found land. It was new only to the visitors, which is a bit cheeky when you think about it.
audio/g6/s/in-labrador-the-mainland-part: In Labrador, the mainland part of this province, the Innu and the Inuit live on their homelands today.
audio/g6/s/it-has-carried-people-up-and-: It has carried people up and down since 1879. Léa says it is le funiculaire. I say it is my new favourite word.
audio/g6/s/it-is-a-very-old-meeg-maw-des: It is a very old Meeg-maw design. You can see it today in quillwork and beadwork, and on jackets and buildings. Many people connect it with the sun.
audio/g6/s/jee-book-took-was-a-meeg-maw-: Jee-book-took was a Meeg-maw gathering place long before there was a city. The British built Halifax here in 1749 without asking the Meeg-mah.
audio/g6/s/l-a-says-about-nine-out-of-ev: Léa says about nine out of every ten people in this city speak French first. It has been spoken here for more than 400 years.
audio/g6/s/last-test-three-right-answers: Last test! Three right answers and it is time to say goodbye.
audio/g6/s/lodie-calls-the-tide-la-mar-e: Élodie calls the tide la marée. The water takes about six hours to go from high to low, and then it turns and comes back. She has a tide gauge. Shall we read it?
audio/g6/s/lodie-has-some-numbers-to-sha: Élodie has some numbers to share. Three right answers and you choose what we do next.
audio/g6/s/lodie-says-acadian-farmers-fi: Élodie says Acadian farmers first built walls like this one more than 300 years ago. People around here still look after them. Clock, show us how it began!
audio/g6/s/long-before-the-french-city-a: Long before the French city, a St. Lawrence Iroquoian village called Stad-uh-koh-nuh stood right here. Today the Huron-Wendat community of Wen-dah-keh is right beside Quebec City.
audio/g6/s/look-at-the-land-along-the-sh: Look at the land along the shore. The fields are not squares. They are long thin strips, like ribbons, all running back from the water.
audio/g6/s/make-a-fair-trade-three-right: Make a fair trade. Three right answers and we head up the cliff.
audio/g6/s/many-settle-at-a-place-called: Many settle at a place called Birchtown. They were given less land than they were promised, and poorer land too. They built their homes and communities anyway.
audio/g6/s/measure-the-long-thin-lots-th: Measure the long thin lots. Three right answers and we fly over the fields of today.
audio/g6/s/measure-the-slanted-fields-th: Measure the slanted fields. Three right answers and the window opens again.
audio/g6/s/meeg-maw-is-the-word-for-one-: Meeg-maw is the word for one person, and for the language too. All the people together are the Meeg-mah.
audio/g6/s/merci-l-a-and-au-revoir-that-: Merci, Léa. And au revoir. That means goodbye, or really, until we see each other again.
audio/g6/s/merci-lodie-she-keeps-her-lan: Merci, Élodie! She keeps her language, her flag and her family's stories alive, and she showed me that good walls take good neighbours.
audio/g6/s/merci-olivier-next-we-sail-fo: Merci, Olivier! Next we sail for the Acadian shore of Nova Scotia, where people won farmland from the sea. Yes, really. Tick tock!
audio/g6/s/mud-in-french-is-la-boue-by-t: Mud in French is la boue. By the time we got back, my feet were two mud puddings. The tide arrived right on time.
audio/g6/s/nearly-at-the-top-three-right: Nearly at the top. Three right answers finishes the chapter.
audio/g6/s/newfoundland-did-not-join-can: Newfoundland did not join Canada until 1949. It was the last province to join. Now then, how much salt fish fits in a bin?
audio/g6/s/next-the-balloon-follows-the-: Next the balloon follows the coast to Halifax, a busy harbour on the sea. Back into the basket I go. Tick tock!
audio/g6/s/no-it-is-the-tide-twice-a-day: No, it is the tide. Twice a day the sea rises and falls. In the My-nus Basin it can change by as much as about 16 metres, as tall as a five-storey building.
audio/g6/s/now-up-citadel-hill-at-the-to: Now up Citadel Hill! At the top sits the Citadel, a star-shaped fort with thick walls, built to guard the harbour. The view is enormous.
audio/g6/s/off-we-hop-over-the-water-fro: Off we hop, over the water from Halifax. The clock keeps pointing east, and east, and east. Until there is almost nothing left to point at.
audio/g6/s/olivier-gave-me-a-little-tin-: Olivier gave me a little tin of le sirop d'érable, which is maple syrup. It is the best thing I have ever put on a pancake.
audio/g6/s/olivier-s-family-still-makes-: Olivier's family still makes maple sugar today.
audio/g6/s/on-the-community-building-is-: On the community building is a big eight-pointed star, in red, yellow, white and black. Sadie has a little one on her jacket too. The Meeg-mah have used this star for a very long time.
audio/g6/s/on-the-sea-cliffs-nearby-puff: On the sea cliffs nearby, puffins are nesting too. But first, some iceberg sums with Declan.
audio/g6/s/once-rain-washes-the-salt-awa: Once rain washes the salt away, the soil grows rich crops. The Acadians live as neighbours of the Meeg-mah. You say it meeg-mah. They have lived here for thousands of years.
audio/g6/s/one-last-set-of-puzzles-for-t: One last set of puzzles for the day. Three right answers finishes the chapter.
audio/g6/s/one-last-set-of-questions-for: One last set of questions for this grade. Three right answers and we reach the very edge.
audio/g6/s/only-about-one-tenth-of-an-ic: Only about one tenth of an iceberg shows above the water. The other nine tenths hide below the waves.
audio/g6/s/out-on-the-river-the-water-is: Out on the river the water is getting wider, and it is slowly turning salty. The sea is not far now.
audio/g6/s/pack-the-salt-fish-three-righ: Pack the salt fish. Three right answers and Declan lets you choose what we do next.
audio/g6/s/paddles-up-a-canoe-is-waiting: Paddles up! A canoe is waiting by the water, and Sadie shows me how to paddle with my wings tucked in. Dip, pull, dip, pull. I only splashed myself twice.
audio/g6/s/read-l-a-s-map-three-right-an: Read Léa's map. Three right answers and the window opens again.
audio/g6/s/read-lodie-s-tide-gauge-three: Read Élodie's tide gauge. Three right answers and the window opens again.
audio/g6/s/sadie-goes-to-school-and-she-: Sadie goes to school, and she is learning the Meeg-maw language from her grandmother. This is how she says hello. Gway! You say it gway. I said it back, and I think I got it right. Mostly.
audio/g6/s/sadie-has-two-ideas-for-the-a: Sadie has two ideas for the afternoon. Shall we paddle a canoe on the lake, or walk the shore trail to look for eagles?
audio/g6/s/sadie-says-a-treaty-is-a-prom: Sadie says a treaty is a promise you keep looking after. So is beadwork. She likes things neat, so she brought her beads.
audio/g6/s/sadie-walks-us-along-the-shor: Sadie walks us along the shore. A bald eagle circles over the lake, and little boats bob on the water. I waved. The eagle ignored me.
audio/g6/s/sail-the-ocean-with-champlain: Sail the ocean with Champlain. Three right answers and we climb to the walls.
audio/g6/s/see-that-long-green-bank-besi: See that long green bank beside the water? It is a dyke, a wall of earth that keeps the sea out of the farms. In French it is la digue. Let's find a guide!
audio/g6/s/see-the-cone-shaped-homes-eac: See the cone-shaped homes? Each one is a wee-goo-om. You say it wee-goo-om. It is made of poles covered with birchbark. And look at the canoes. Their sides rise in the middle, to keep out ocean waves.
audio/g6/s/shaw-nuh-dith-it-the-last-kno: Shaw-nuh-dith-it, the last known Bee-oth-uk, died in St. John's in 1829. Before she died she drew maps and pictures, so that her people's story would not be lost.
audio/g6/s/she-says-the-castle-is-really: She says the castle is really a hotel, called the Château Frontenac. But the river is the real star.
audio/g6/s/so-thank-you-l-a-olivier-lodi: So thank you, Léa, Olivier, Élodie, Sadie, Amara and Declan. Each of you showed me a piece of the east, and I learned so much.
audio/g6/s/so-they-build-a-wall-of-earth: So they build a wall of earth to hold the sea back. Through the wall is a wooden gate called an aboiteau. Rain water flows out at low tide, and the rising tide pushes the gate shut.
audio/g6/s/some-acadian-families-escaped: Some Acadian families escaped into the woods. Meeg-maw families sheltered them and helped them survive.
audio/g6/s/thank-you-amara-halifax-has-w: Thank you, Amara. Halifax has welcomed new people for a very long time, and it still does. Au revoir!
audio/g6/s/thank-you-sadie-for-showing-m: Thank you, Sadie, for showing me your home today. It was a big treat to meet someone who lives in the place we have been looking at through the window.
audio/g6/s/that-blue-lake-is-the-bras-d-: That blue lake is the Bras d'Or Lake. It is salty like the sea, even though it sits in the middle of the island. Down we go!
audio/g6/s/that-is-the-st-lawrence-l-a-c: That is the St. Lawrence. Léa calls it le fleuve, the river. It runs all the way to the ocean, and for a long time it was the only road there was. Clock, show us!
audio/g6/s/the-acadians-and-the-meeg-mah: The Acadians and the Meeg-mah lived side by side for more than a hundred years. They traded, shared what they knew, and some families married into each other.
audio/g6/s/the-acadians-farmed-the-salt-: The Acadians farmed the salt marshes, which left the Meeg-maw hunting grounds alone. How long does a dyke take?
audio/g6/s/the-balloon-is-tugging-east-a: The balloon is tugging east, along the coast to Cape Breton Island, in Meeg-mah-gee, the homeland of the Meeg-mah. Our next chapter is The People of the Dawn.
audio/g6/s/the-captain-calls-out-b-y-whi: The captain calls out b'y, which is a Newfoundland word for a friend or a buddy. Declan says he calls everybody b'y. Even me. Even, probably, the iceberg.
audio/g6/s/the-clock-is-pointing-across-: The clock is pointing across the water, to the big island of Newfoundland, right at the edge of the map. One more hop and we are there. Tick tock!
audio/g6/s/the-crews-salted-the-fish-and: The crews salted the fish and dried it on wooden racks called flakes. Little fishing villages, called outports, grew up all around the coast.
audio/g6/s/the-french-wanted-beaver-furs: The French wanted beaver furs, to make hats back in France. First Nations hunters and traders brought the furs, and traded them for things like kettles, cloth and blankets.
audio/g6/s/the-funicular-it-is-a-little-: The funicular it is! A little glass cabin that rides up the cliff on rails.
audio/g6/s/the-little-fort-grew-into-a-t: The little fort grew into a town, and the town became the heart of New France.
audio/g6/s/the-meeg-mah-are-one-of-the-w: The Meeg-mah are one of the Wabanaki nations. That name is often translated as People of the Dawn, because their homelands are in the east, where the dawn comes early. Early birds, just like me.
audio/g6/s/the-meeg-mah-call-this-island: The Meeg-mah call this island Oo-nah-mah-gee. You say Meeg-mah like meeg-mah, and Oo-nah-mah-gee like oo-nah-mah-gee.
audio/g6/s/the-meeg-mah-have-known-this-: The Meeg-mah have known this harbour since long before any ship came, and they know it still. Their name for it is usually written Jee-book-took, which means the great harbour. You say it jee-book-took.
audio/g6/s/the-meeg-mah-have-lived-here-: The Meeg-mah have lived here too, for a long time, and they are still here today. Their name for the island is Ook-dah-hum-gook.
audio/g6/s/the-old-town-is-at-the-top-of: The old town is at the top of the cliff, and we are at the bottom. Léa says there are two ways up. Which shall we take?
audio/g6/s/the-river-keeps-going-east-an: The river keeps going east, and so shall we. But that is another chapter. Tick tock!
audio/g6/s/the-roads-run-along-the-river: The roads run along the river now, but the old lot lines are still there to see. Olivier's family farm is one of those thin ribbons.
audio/g6/s/the-sea-in-french-is-la-mer-f: The sea in French is la mer. For a little while the river flowed the other way. I cheered so loudly that a heron left.
audio/g6/s/the-soldiers-order-the-acadia: The soldiers order the Acadians to leave their homes. Families are put on ships, and many are split up. This is called the Deportation, or le Grand Dérangement.
audio/g6/s/the-stairs-it-is-they-are-cal: The stairs it is! They are called the Breakneck Stairs, and they are the oldest stairs in the city.
audio/g6/s/the-sun-is-going-down-and-the: The sun is going down, and the harbour glows. Out on the rocks, a red and white lighthouse keeps watch over the water. In French that is le phare.
audio/g6/s/the-sun-sinks-low-over-the-hi: The sun sinks low over the hills, and the whole lake glows. Sadie says the dawn will come early to her land again tomorrow, as it always does.
audio/g6/s/the-tide-is-on-the-move-lodie: The tide is on the move! Élodie says there are two ways to see it. Which shall we choose?
audio/g6/s/the-window-again-and-it-is-la: The window again, and it is late winter long ago. Look at the buckets hanging on the trees! These are maple trees, and the sap inside them is sweet.
audio/g6/s/the-window-fades-about-10-000: The window fades. About 10,000 people were sent away over the next years. Some found their way back, years later. Others made new homes far away, as far as Louisiana.
audio/g6/s/the-window-into-the-past-it-i: The window into the past! It is about 1,000 years ago, at the northern tip of the island. A longship with a striped sail has just landed.
The window into the past! It is the late 1600s. Acadians, French-speaking settlers, are farming here. But this land is salt marsh, and the sea floods it twice a day.
audio/g6/s/the-window-into-the-past-the-: The window into the past! The year is 1608. A French explorer named Samuel de Champlain has just built a wooden fort right here, at the foot of the cliff.
The window into the past! The year is about 1700, in New France. See the land? It is cut into long, narrow lots, and every lot touches the river.
The window into the past. The year is 1783. The American Revolution is over, and ships are bringing thousands of people to Nova Scotia.
audio/g6/s/the-window-into-the-past-this: The window into the past! This is a summer camp by the shore, long before any ships came. The Meeg-mah have lived on this land for more than 10,000 years.
audio/g6/s/the-window-shows-a-sadder-tim: The window shows a sadder time. The year is 1755. Britain and France are rivals for this land, and British soldiers have come to the Acadian villages.
audio/g6/s/these-are-the-norse-also-call: These are the Norse, also called Vikings. They sailed from Greenland and built a small village of sod houses at Lance oh Meadows. The roofs are made of grass!
audio/g6/s/these-are-the-peace-and-frien: These are the Peace and Friendship Treaties, made between the Meeg-mah and the British Crown in the 1700s. The Meeg-mah did not give up their land in them.
audio/g6/s/these-long-farms-were-laid-ou: These long farms were laid out along riverbanks that were already the homelands of First Nations. They had lived, fished and travelled along this river for thousands of years.
audio/g6/s/they-are-the-first-europeans-: They are the first Europeans known to reach North America, about 500 years before Columbus.
audio/g6/s/they-come-for-the-cod-the-gra: They come for the cod. The Grand Banks, just off this coast, were full of huge schools of fish. In French, cod is la morue.
audio/g6/s/this-is-amara-her-grandparent: This is Amara. Her grandparents came to Canada by ship, and they landed in this very harbour. Now she lives a short walk from the water.
audio/g6/s/this-is-declan-he-lives-right: This is Declan. He lives right here in St. John's, in a bright orange house on one of those very steep streets. His legs are very strong.
audio/g6/s/this-is-halifax-in-nova-scoti: This is Halifax, in Nova Scotia. It is one of the great natural harbours of the world, and its water stays free of ice all year.
audio/g6/s/this-is-l-a-she-has-lived-her: This is Léa. She has lived here all her life, and she speaks French at home and at school.
audio/g6/s/this-is-lodie-she-is-an-acadi: This is Élodie. She is an Acadian girl, and she speaks French at home. Her family has lived beside this bay for a very long time.
audio/g6/s/this-is-newfoundland-an-islan: This is Newfoundland, an island on the edge of the sea. The city below is St. John's. Look at the houses! Red, yellow, blue and green, stacked up the steep hill like a box of crayons.
audio/g6/s/this-is-olivier-he-lives-on-a: This is Olivier. He lives on a farm by the river, with strawberry rows, apple trees, and a wood full of maple trees. He speaks French at home and at school.
audio/g6/s/this-is-quebec-city-it-is-one: This is Quebec City. It is one of the oldest cities in all of North America. And nearly everyone here speaks French.
audio/g6/s/this-is-the-acadian-shore-of-: This is the Acadian shore of Nova Scotia. The sea goes out so far here that the boats sit on the mud. I landed in a puddle. A very big puddle.
audio/g6/s/time-for-the-farm-stand-three: Time for the farm stand. Three right answers finishes the chapter.
audio/g6/s/to-protect-it-people-built-st: To protect it, people built stone walls all the way around. They are still here! Quebec is the only city north of Mexico that has kept its old walls.
audio/g6/s/today-the-building-is-the-can: Today the building is the Canadian Museum of Immigration at Pier 21, and anyone can visit. For now, the clerk needs help with his tally.
audio/g6/s/up-the-hill-we-go-just-in-tim: Up the hill we go, just in time! The gun fires at twelve o'clock, and Amara covers her ears. BOOM! I covered mine too, with my wings.
audio/g6/s/up-the-shore-trail-we-go-unde: Up the shore trail we go, under the spruce trees, with our eyes on the sky. A bald eagle glides right over us, as wide as a door.
audio/g6/s/wait-the-clock-on-the-balloon: Wait! The clock on the balloon is spinning! Its hands swing all the way round and point west. The prairies and the mountains are waiting for us.
audio/g6/s/we-are-at-olivier-s-sugar-sha: We are at Olivier's sugar shack, which he calls la cabane à sucre. Steam is pouring out of the roof! What shall we do first?
audio/g6/s/we-are-just-east-of-quebec-ci: We are just east of Quebec City, where farms have lined this river for hundreds of years. I see a windmill and a farmhouse. I wave at the farmhouse. It does not wave back.
audio/g6/s/we-made-it-to-the-top-what-a-: We made it to the top. What a view! The whole river, and ships still sailing for the sea.
audio/g6/s/we-waited-on-the-riverbank-th: We waited on the riverbank. Then we heard it! The sea came rushing up the river in a wave, pushing against the current. It is called a tidal bore.
audio/g6/s/we-walk-the-cliff-path-and-th: We walk the cliff path, and there they are! Puffins sit on the grassy ledges, with black backs, white fronts, orange feet and great big orange beaks.
audio/g6/s/what-a-place-the-sea-goes-out: What a place! The sea goes out and comes back twice a day, and the Acadians are still here, farming the land their families dyked long ago.
audio/g6/s/when-it-flies-off-sadie-waves: When it flies off, Sadie waves and says nem-ool-tes. You say it nem-ool-tes. It means see you again. I said it too, in case the eagle was listening.
audio/g6/s/when-we-reach-the-shore-again: When we reach the shore again, Sadie says weh-lah-lin. You say it weh-lah-lin. It means thank you. I say it right back, for the paddling lesson.
audio/g6/s/why-so-long-and-thin-olivier-: Why so long and thin? Olivier says the river holds the secret. Clock, show us!
audio/g6/s/you-may-know-it-as-cape-breto: You may know it as Cape Breton Island. The Meeg-mah have lived here for more than 10,000 years, and they live here today.
audio/g6/s/you-walk-in-through-a-great-s: You walk in through a great stone gate. Léa says a gate is la porte. The walls are 4.6 kilometres around. Léa has a map. Shall we measure?
audio/g7/s/a-bone-is-l-os-i-measured-the: A bone is l'os. I measured the jaw, and Pip measured my tape measure. Both of us got a number, and neither of us got eaten.
audio/g7/s/a-boy-is-waiting-by-a-fence-p: A boy is waiting by a fence post. This is Tyson. He is Nakoda, also called Uh-sin-ih-boyn, and he lives in southern Saskatchewan. His people have lived on these plains for a very long time.
audio/g7/s/a-fork-in-a-river-is-la-fourc: A fork in a river is la fourche in French. In winter the rivers freeze solid, and Kai skates on a trail that runs along the ice, right through the middle of the city!
audio/g7/s/a-girl-in-a-teal-hoodie-is-wa: A girl in a teal hoodie is waving. This is Priya. She lives in Drumheller, and she volunteers at the Royal Teer-ul Museum, which is packed with dinosaur bones.
audio/g7/s/a-train-whistle-toots-from-th: A train whistle toots from the old station, and out hops Dot, a small purple dinosaur in a blue driver's cap! Pip squeaks. Dot says choo choo. It is plenty.
audio/g7/s/about-30-million-bison-fewer-: About 30 million bison. Fewer than 1,000 by the late 1880s, in one lifetime. The numbers tell the story, so let us look at them carefully. Three right answers and we come back to today.
audio/g7/s/after-1869-as-canada-took-ove: After 1869, as Canada took over this land, the May-tee had to stand up for their homes and their rights, led by Louis Riel. In the years that followed, many families were pushed off their river lots.
audio/g7/s/ah-nish-ih-nah-bay-families-b: Ah-nish-ih-nah-bay families built the birchbark canoes, a canoe is un canot. They supplied food such as wild rice and maple sugar, and they guided the brigades. They also trapped furs and traded them.
audio/g7/s/ahead-is-the-biggest-lake-of-: Ahead is the biggest lake of them all, Lake Superior. At its western end a river called the Kam-in-iss-tih-kwah runs into it, and the city of Thunder Bay sits beside the water.
audio/g7/s/and-creeping-along-behind-the: And creeping along behind them is an Albertosaurus, a meat-eater and a smaller cousin of T. rex. It was about 9 metres long. Pip hid behind me. I hid behind Pip. Time for some very big numbers.
audio/g7/s/and-look-at-the-carts-their-w: And look at the carts! Their wheels are as tall as a person. Let's measure one.
audio/g7/s/and-the-dark-speck-it-is-a-bi: And the dark speck? It is a bison. Many people say buffalo, but bison is the proper name. In French it is le bison. A big one just looked at me, so I looked back. Politely.
audio/g7/s/archaeologists-who-dig-up-the: Archaeologists, who dig up the past very carefully, have found old campfires, tools and fish bones right here. People camped here, fished here and came back year after year.
audio/g7/s/back-in-the-present-tyson-cro: Back in the present, Tyson crouches and parts the grass with his fingers. It looks plain, but it is tougher than it looks. I tried to pull one blade out and fell over backwards.
audio/g7/s/back-in-today-kai-walks-us-to: Back in today! Kai walks us to the footbridge. The sun is going down, and the two rivers shine like copper kettles.
audio/g7/s/back-on-the-wharf-the-lake-is: Back on the wharf, the lake is turning gold. Zoe says mee-gwetch, which is thank you in Ah-nish-ih-nah-bay-moh-win, the Ah-nish-ih-nah-bay language. I say it back. Mine comes out like a sneeze.
audio/g7/s/back-to-the-window-and-now-it: Back to the window, and now it is the 1930s. I will tell this one plainly. The rain stopped, year after year, and the fields turned dry.
audio/g7/s/back-to-today-jade-has-brough: Back to today! Jade has brought me to a Red River cart, built the old way. In French it is la charrette, and its wheels are taller than I am.
audio/g7/s/back-to-today-on-the-wharf-at: Back to today, on the wharf at Fort William Historical Park. The people who work here dress like 1815, and one of them is wearing a red toque and a sash and carrying a load. Zoe says that is the full outfit.
audio/g7/s/back-to-today-priya-shows-us-: Back to today! Priya shows us a striped cliff. Each stripe is a layer of rock, like the pages of a book. The lower pages are older.
audio/g7/s/back-to-today-the-arrows-show: Back to today! The arrows show which way the water goes. The Red River flows north, away from the United States, toward Lake Winnipeg. A river is la rivière.
audio/g7/s/below-us-is-grasslands-nation: Below us is Grasslands National Park, one of the last big pieces of native prairie in Canada. And what is that dark speck, moving slowly through the grass? Down we go to find out.
audio/g7/s/bison-keep-the-grassland-heal: Bison keep the grassland healthy by grazing and by rolling in the dust, which is called wallowing. But most of Canada's native prairie has been ploughed up for farms and towns. What is left is precious.
audio/g7/s/both-of-them-have-a-point-now: Both of them have a point. Now for some price puzzles. Three right answers and you pick the post where we trade.
audio/g7/s/count-and-share-the-load-thre: Count and share the load. Three right answers and the window opens again.
audio/g7/s/count-the-years-with-priya-th: Count the years with Priya. Three right answers and each one pays a Made Beaver, then we look at the rocks.
audio/g7/s/dot-brakes-beside-a-little-to: Dot brakes beside a little town, and a boy waves from the gravel by the track. This is Lukas. His family grows wheat and canola on a farm just outside town.
audio/g7/s/dot-lets-me-pull-the-whistle-: Dot lets me pull the whistle cord. Toot toot! The cows in the next field did not even look up. They have heard it all before.
audio/g7/s/dot-s-cars-are-being-loaded-a: Dot's cars are being loaded, and the bins need measuring. Three right answers and the window opens again.
audio/g7/s/dot-s-train-rolls-up-beside-a: Dot's train rolls up beside a tall wooden building. This is a grain elevator. Farmers hauled their wheat here, where it was weighed, lifted to the top and stored in tall bins.
audio/g7/s/dot-waves-me-into-the-engine-: Dot waves me into the engine, and the whole train rumbles out of town with its long line of grain cars behind us. I looked back and could not see the end of it.
audio/g7/s/every-bundle-is-a-pi-ce-packe: Every bundle is a pièce, packed to weigh about 90 pounds, or about 41 kilograms. A voyageur carried two at a time over a portage. I lifted one and turned into a very short owl.
audio/g7/s/every-summer-came-the-rendezv: Every summer came the Rendezvous, a huge meeting. Big canoes from Montreal paddled in with trade goods from the east. Smaller canoes came down from the far northwest, full of furs.
audio/g7/s/everyone-here-talks-about-le-: Everyone here talks about le castor, the beaver, because beaver fur is what everyone wants. The beaver would much rather keep its coat.
audio/g7/s/first-nations-peoples-met-her: First Nations peoples met here to trade, fish and make agreements, among them the ancestors of the Cree, the Ah-nish-ih-nah-bay, the Nakoda and the Dakota. Goods travelled huge distances on the rivers.
audio/g7/s/for-the-plains-nations-the-bi: For the Plains nations the bison is much more than food. Tipi covers are made of its hide. So are clothes. Tools are made of bone and horn, and dried dung is fuel for the fire. Nothing is wasted.
audio/g7/s/for-thousands-of-years-this-l: For thousands of years this land had been covered in prairie grass with deep roots. Farmers had ploughed much of it under. Without those roots, the dry soil turned to dust, and the wind carried it away.
audio/g7/s/from-lake-winnipeg-the-water-: From Lake Winnipeg the water keeps going north through more rivers, all the way to Hudson Bay. That is why trading companies wanted this spot. Boats could reach the bay from here.
audio/g7/s/goodbye-kai-my-clock-balloon-: Goodbye, Kai! My clock balloon has drifted just across the Red River from The Forks, to the part of Winnipeg called St. Boniface.
audio/g7/s/goodbye-zoe-and-goodbye-voyag: Goodbye, Zoe, and goodbye, voyageurs! My clock balloon has floated far west from Lake Superior, over forest, rock and lakes, and now the land has gone flat and the sky is enormous.
audio/g7/s/help-jade-scale-up-a-pemmican: Help Jade scale up a pemmican recipe. Three right answers and then you choose how to spend the afternoon.
audio/g7/s/huge-black-dust-storms-rolled: Huge black dust storms rolled over the farms. Crops failed, families lost their farms, and many people packed up and left.
audio/g7/s/hunters-work-together-and-one: Hunters work together, and one way is to drive a herd over a cliff or into a strong pen called a pound. Everyone in the camp has a job to do. Tyson says it is time for some big numbers.
audio/g7/s/i-can-almost-hear-the-axles-b: I can almost hear the axles. Back into the basket I go, and we follow the carts west to The Sea of Grass. Tick tock!
audio/g7/s/i-climb-into-the-box-and-jade: I climb into the box, and Jade walks beside the ox. The big wooden wheels creak and squeal, and the whole cart bounces along.
audio/g7/s/i-try-the-step-with-my-big-ow: I try the step with my big owl feet. The fiddle is le violon in French. It was the only one of us that stayed in time.
audio/g7/s/in-1885-farther-west-at-buh-t: In 1885, farther west at Buh-tosh on the South Saskatchewan River, the May-tee again asked Canada to respect their land, and again were not heard.
audio/g7/s/in-2005-bison-were-brought-ba: In 2005 bison were brought back to Grasslands National Park, and now a herd of several hundred lives here. We bounce along in a ranger's truck and stop on a hill to look.
audio/g7/s/in-between-are-stripes-of-bri: In between are stripes of bright yellow. That is canola, and it is in flower in July. We are on the Alberta prairie, east of the Rocky Mountains, in farm country.
audio/g7/s/in-french-a-farm-is-la-ferme-: In French, a farm is la ferme. Lukas learned it at school. He says it is easier to spell than combine.
audio/g7/s/in-return-canada-promised-res: In return, Canada promised reserve land, yearly payments, schools, farm tools and help with farming. In Treaty 6 it also promised medicine, and help in times of hunger.
audio/g7/s/inside-the-museum-lab-stands-: Inside the museum lab stands a whole skeleton on a stand, with scale models of its bones on the table. Priya hands me a tape measure, and I stretch it along the floor with great importance.
audio/g7/s/it-grew-from-the-families-of-: It grew from the families of First Nations women (often Cree and Ah-nish-ih-nah-bay) and French and Scottish fur traders. Then, over generations, May-tee families married one another and became a new people, a nation.
audio/g7/s/it-is-also-the-territory-of-t: It is also the territory of the neighbouring Treaty 7 nations, the Soo-tih-nah and the Stoney Nakoda. It is a homeland of the May-tee too. They live in Alberta today.
audio/g7/s/it-is-built-entirely-of-wood-: It is built entirely of wood and hide, with no iron and no nails, so it could be mended anywhere on the prairie.
audio/g7/s/jade-has-two-ideas-for-the-af: Jade has two ideas for the afternoon. Shall we learn a step of the Red River Jig, or ride in the Red River cart?
audio/g7/s/jade-says-hello-like-this-tah: Jade says hello like this: tahn-shee! I said it back. She says I had a good try, and she is a very kind fiddler.
audio/g7/s/jade-tucks-her-fiddle-under-h: Jade tucks her fiddle under her chin and plays the Red River Jig, while her feet go tap, tap, tap. The jig is quick and bouncy, and the steps match the beat of the tune.
audio/g7/s/kai-says-people-have-been-mee: Kai says people have been meeting at this very spot for thousands of years. That is a long time to wait for a snack. Clock, show us!
audio/g7/s/kai-says-the-story-of-the-fur: Kai says the story of the fur trade did not end at the trading posts. Around these rivers a new people grew up, often with a First Nations mother and a European father. They are the May-tee.
audio/g7/s/last-puzzles-of-the-day-three: Last puzzles of the day. Three right answers finishes the chapter.
audio/g7/s/last-stop-this-morning-i-left: Last stop! This morning I left the Badlands on Dot's little train. She is the driver, her cars are full of grain, and I am sitting on top of one of them holding my hat.
audio/g7/s/learn-the-fur-trade-money-thr: Learn the fur trade money. Three right answers and the window opens on a trading post, about the year 1815, where two people will tell us what they see.
audio/g7/s/let-s-measure-a-homestead-the: Let's measure a homestead the way Lukas's family does, in hectares. Three right answers and we go to see the train.
audio/g7/s/look-at-the-long-narrow-strip: Look at the long, narrow strips of land running back from the water. These are river lots, and you can still see their shapes along this river today.
audio/g7/s/look-down-two-rivers-are-runn: Look down! Two rivers are running together like the letter Y. This is the middle of Winnipeg, in Manitoba, at a place called The Forks.
audio/g7/s/lukas-s-great-great-grandpare: Lukas's great-great-grandparents came here from Ukraine more than 120 years ago to start that farm. Today his mom drives the combine, and Lukas helps in the busy weeks.
audio/g7/s/lukas-s-mom-is-about-to-cut-t: Lukas's mom is about to cut the wheat, and Dot's train is about to leave with a full load. Shall we ride in the combine harvester, or in the engine of the grain train?
audio/g7/s/lukas-taught-me-how-to-say-it: Lukas taught me how to say it in Ukrainian: dyah-koo-yoo. You say it dyah-koo-yoo. Then Dot pulled her whistle, and her little train turned back east with its grain, on the way to the ports.
audio/g7/s/many-of-those-promises-were-b: Many of those promises were broken or only half kept. For many years people on reserves needed a written pass from a government agent just to leave. The treaties are still in force today, and the nations are still here.
audio/g7/s/may-tee-people-worked-as-guid: May-tee people worked as guides, interpreters and canoe crews too. Without all of them the canoes went nowhere. That is just a plain fact.
audio/g7/s/measure-the-cart-wheels-three: Measure the cart wheels. Three right answers, and each one earns you a Made Beaver on the way.
audio/g7/s/nests-with-eggs-and-even-tiny: Nests with eggs, and even tiny babies, have been found in southern Alberta, at a place called Devil's Coulee. An egg is l'œuf in French. Pip is staring at the eggs and not blinking.
audio/g7/s/next-stop-is-wheat-and-sky-wh: Next stop is Wheat and Sky, where gold fields stretch all the way to the edge of the world. All aboard! Tick tock!
audio/g7/s/now-pip-here-is-the-big-secre: Now Pip, here is the big secret. Birds are living dinosaurs, descended from small feathered meat-eaters. Priya points to a chickadee on the fence. That tiny bird is a dinosaur.
audio/g7/s/now-the-sums-for-our-own-cano: Now the sums for our own canoe. Three right answers finishes the chapter.
audio/g7/s/once-there-were-about-6-000-o: Once there were about 6,000 of these wooden elevators on the prairies. Now only a few hundred are left, so Dot toots her whistle at this one every time.
audio/g7/s/one-cart-could-carry-about-40: One cart could carry about 400 kilograms. At a river, the wheels came off and the cart floated across like a little boat.
audio/g7/s/one-last-set-of-puzzles-for-t: One last set of puzzles for the crew. Three right answers finishes the chapter.
audio/g7/s/one-last-set-of-puzzles-from-: One last set of puzzles from our ride. Three right answers finishes the chapter, and the whole grade.
audio/g7/s/out-here-the-land-is-as-flat-: Out here the land is as flat as a pancake and as gold as a pancake too. It is a whole sea of wheat, which the French call le blé, all the way to the sky.
audio/g7/s/out-of-the-east-the-clock-fol: Out of the east the clock follows the old cart trails, past the Red River and on and on, until the trees give up. Then there is only sky. Hold on to your hat, because the wind out here wants it.
audio/g7/s/people-came-from-ukraine-germ: People came from Ukraine, Germany, Scandinavia, Britain, the United States, Iceland and many other places. There were few trees, so the first home was often a sod house, made of blocks of prairie turf.
audio/g7/s/people-speak-mee-chif-a-langu: People speak Mee-chif, a language that weaves Cree and French together. And the May-tee flag flies, a white infinity sign on blue, flown by 1816. It is one of the oldest flags that began in Canada.
audio/g7/s/pip-did-not-find-the-lost-egg: Pip did not find the lost eggs. But Pip found a whole world of cousins, and every chickadee in Alberta is now a celebrity. Pip waves goodbye with both arms.
audio/g7/s/prairie-grass-hides-its-best-: Prairie grass hides its best part underground. The roots go down a metre or more and hold the soil in place. That is why the grass survives drought, fire and hungry animals. In French it is l'herbe.
audio/g7/s/priya-has-two-jobs-for-the-af: Priya has two jobs for the afternoon. Shall we join the dig crew and brush a bone out of the ground, or go into the museum lab and measure a skeleton?
audio/g7/s/priya-needs-help-with-models-: Priya needs help with models, drawings and maps. Three right answers and the window opens again.
audio/g7/s/priya-says-this-is-the-best-p: Priya says this is the best place in the world for old eggs. Pip's eyes go round. Pip says one word, eggs. A dinosaur is le dinosaure in French.
audio/g7/s/priya-waved-at-pip-first-i-am: Priya waved at Pip first. I am not jealous. I am a little jealous.
audio/g7/s/riel-was-tried-for-treason-an: Riel was tried for treason and hanged in Regina on November 16, 1885. Today Manitoba honours him as its founder, with Louis Riel Day every February.
audio/g7/s/rivers-were-the-highways-thre: Rivers were the highways. Three right answers and we look at the rivers today.
