audio/g7/s/rock-is-la-roche-i-brushed-so: Rock is la roche. I brushed so carefully that a beetle thanked me. Then it sat on my beak. Palaeontologists say that is a good sign.
audio/g7/s/see-that-flat-topped-headland: See that flat-topped headland out on the lake? People call it the Sleeping Giant. And near the river is a wooden fort with a flag. Down we go!
audio/g7/s/see-those-tall-pillars-with-f: See those tall pillars with flat stones balanced on top like hats? Those are hoodoos. And one of the rocks down there just moved. I think. Down we go!
audio/g7/s/so-we-do-a-portage-that-means: So we do a portage. That means everyone lifts the canoe and the pièces and carries them over land. I carry the map. It weighs nothing, and it is still too heavy.
audio/g7/s/solve-the-canoe-sums-three-ri: Solve the canoe sums. Three right answers and then we pick a canoe to ride in.
audio/g7/s/some-rings-are-hundreds-of-ye: Some rings are hundreds of years old, or even older, and they are still on the land today. We leave every stone where it lies. A circle in French is le cercle.
audio/g7/s/somebody-down-there-is-playin: Somebody down there is playing a fiddle, and it sounds very cheerful. I tapped my foot so hard that I nearly fell out of the basket.
audio/g7/s/thank-you-jade-you-showed-me-: Thank you, Jade! You showed me that the May-tee are a living nation, with music, a language and a flag that still flies today.
audio/g7/s/thank-you-kai-next-we-follow-: Thank you, Kai! Next we follow the river to meet them, in The People of the Red River. Tick tock!
audio/g7/s/thank-you-priya-for-sharing-y: Thank you, Priya, for sharing your backyard. Keep looking down, because after every rain the badlands can show you a brand new bone.
audio/g7/s/thank-you-tyson-for-telling-i: Thank you, Tyson, for telling it plainly. Next the clock tugs us west, to where the land breaks open into strange striped hills full of bones. That is The Land of Giants, the Alberta Badlands. Tick tock!
audio/g7/s/that-place-is-called-the-fork: That place is called The Forks, and it is in Winnipeg. Back into the basket I go. Tick tock!
audio/g7/s/that-wooden-fort-is-fort-will: That wooden fort is Fort William Historical Park. It was built again, just the way it was. Its canoe crews were called les voyageurs. Clock, show us!
audio/g7/s/the-big-ones-were-about-11-me: The big ones were about 11 metres long. The crews swapped cargo and turned around, because the summer was too short for one crew to make the whole trip. Speaking of trips, how fast did they go?
audio/g7/s/the-clock-is-pointing-up-and-: The clock is pointing up and over the mountains, to the Pacific and the far North. But that is another story. Tick tock!
audio/g7/s/the-clock-on-my-balloon-swung: The clock on my balloon swung round and pointed west! So off we float, from Newfoundland, back over Quebec and Ontario, past forests and lakes without end. West is a long way.
audio/g7/s/the-crew-pulls-a-string-grid-: The crew pulls a string grid over the dig site, so every bone is marked by its square. We brush the dust away gently, until a rib shows. Pip spots it first.
audio/g7/s/the-dig-crew-is-marking-out-s: The dig crew is marking out squares. Three right answers and Priya lets us pick our job.
audio/g7/s/the-families-who-stayed-learn: The families who stayed learned to protect the soil. They planted shelter belts of trees, left stubble on the fields and stopped ploughing so deep. Farms still use those ideas today.
audio/g7/s/the-fiddler-is-a-girl-named-j: The fiddler is a girl named Jade. She is May-tee, she lives right here by the river, and she jigs with a dance group.
audio/g7/s/the-hunt-is-very-well-organiz: The hunt is very well organized. Before they start, the hunters elect a captain and agree on a set of rules, the Laws of the Hunt.
audio/g7/s/the-may-tee-are-a-distinct-in: The May-tee are a distinct Indigenous people, with their own history, culture and language. The May-tee Nation grew up in the fur trade country, with its heart right here at the Red River.
audio/g7/s/the-may-tee-are-still-here-wi: The May-tee are still here, with their own language, music and flag, and many May-tee families live in Winnipeg today. Kai says their story starts on the Red River.
audio/g7/s/the-may-tee-nation-is-here-to: The May-tee Nation is here today, one of the three Indigenous peoples named in Canada's Constitution, with First Nations and Inuit.
audio/g7/s/the-meat-is-dried-then-pounde: The meat is dried, then pounded with fat and berries into le pemmican. It keeps for a very long time, and it was the food that fed the whole fur trade.
audio/g7/s/the-north-canoes-did-not-stop: The north canoes did not stop here. They went on west with the cargo from this wharf, up rivers and over portages, toward a place where two rivers meet.
audio/g7/s/the-other-dinosaurs-died-out-: The other dinosaurs died out about 66 million years ago, after a giant asteroid hit the Earth. Pip whispers one word, cousins. Yes, Pip. Cousins.
audio/g7/s/the-plains-nations-are-still-: The Plains nations are still here too. They are raising their children on these grasslands, and working to bring the bison home to their own lands. The grass holds on, and so do the people.
audio/g7/s/the-rangers-count-the-herd-to: The rangers count the herd to see how it is growing, and calves are born every spring. A herd in French is le troupeau. I counted with my wing tips and ran out of wing tips.
audio/g7/s/the-river-from-the-left-is-th: The river from the left is the Uh-sin-ih-boyn. The river from below is the Red. They meet right here and flow on as one. That building with the tower is le marché, the market. I smell snacks.
audio/g7/s/the-steersman-calls-out-en-av: The steersman calls out en avant, which means forward! The paddles all dip together, and I keep time with my feet. I sing off key, and the crew is very polite about it.
audio/g7/s/the-traders-also-needed-one-p: The traders also needed one price list for all those furs. They priced everything in Made Beaver: one good beaver pelt was 1 Made Beaver. You earn them too, for right answers!
audio/g7/s/the-wheel-is-la-roue-in-frenc: The wheel is la roue in French. I count its turns as we roll, because that is what a curious owl does. Jade says I am being silly.
audio/g7/s/the-white-infinity-sign-stand: The white infinity sign stands for two cultures joined together, and for a people that will go on forever.
audio/g7/s/the-window-again-and-now-we-s: The window again, and now we see a people with their own ways. Here is the ceinture fléchée, a long finger-woven sash with many uses. Here are fiddles playing the Red River Jig.
audio/g7/s/the-window-again-now-let-us-l: The window again. Now let us look at whose trade it really was. It depended on First Nations and May-tee people.
audio/g7/s/the-window-again-still-75-mil: The window again, still 75 million years ago, and now we are looking at a nest. Dinosaurs laid eggs! This is a hadrosaur nest, with a mother keeping watch over her little ones.
audio/g7/s/the-window-into-the-past-it-i: The window into the past! It is about 75 million years ago, in a time called the Late Cretaceous. This dry, dusty land is a warm, wet plain beside a shallow inland sea.
The window into the past! It is about the year 1800, and the plains are full of life. Around 30 million bison live on the Great Plains of North America. Try counting that on your fingers.
The window into the past! It is about 1840, and a train of carts is rolling out from the Red River. Each summer, hundreds of May-tee families set out onto the plains for the great bison hunt.

The window into the past! It is about 1900, and the government of Canada is offering settlers 160 acres, a quarter section, for a ten dollar fee. The rules were to live on it, build a house and break the land.
audio/g7/s/the-window-into-the-past-the-: The window into the past! The year is about 1815, and this is Fort William, the great inland headquarters of the North West Company, a fur trade company.
audio/g7/s/the-window-into-the-past-we-a: The window into the past! We are looking back about 6,000 years, long before any fort or any city. No market, no bridge. Just grass, trees and two rivers.
audio/g7/s/the-window-shows-two-trading-: The window shows two trading posts, one on each bank of the river. They are rivals, and each has its own price list. Where shall we trade?
audio/g7/s/the-wooden-axles-were-never-g: The wooden axles were never greased, and they squealed so loudly that you could hear a cart train from far away. Jade covers her ears and laughs.
audio/g7/s/then-a-green-head-pops-up-fro: Then a green head pops up from behind the rock. It is Pip! Pip is a small green dinosaur, and an old friend of mine. Pip has been searching for lost eggs for ages.
audio/g7/s/then-wind-and-rain-wore-the-r: Then wind and rain wore the rock away, bit by bit, and new bones show up every year. In 1884 Joseph Teer-ul found the skull of a big meat-eater near here.
audio/g7/s/there-are-rivers-swamps-and-f: There are rivers, swamps and forests. Duck-billed dinosaurs called hadrosaurs munch the leaves. Horned dinosaurs with bony frills, like Centrosaurus, wander by.
audio/g7/s/they-paddled-14-hours-a-day-o: They paddled 14 hours a day or more, and they sang to keep the stroke together. I would sing too, if it meant I did not have to carry anything.
audio/g7/s/they-took-up-arms-with-louis-: They took up arms, with Louis Riel as their leader and Gabriel Dumont leading the fighters. Canada sent soldiers west by the new railway. After four days of fighting at Buh-tosh, the May-tee were defeated.
audio/g7/s/thirty-million-is-a-very-big-: Thirty million is a very big number. Three right answers and we look at the ground under our feet.
audio/g7/s/this-is-kai-he-lives-in-winni: This is Kai. He lives in Winnipeg, and he comes to The Forks almost every week to eat at the market, walk along the river and watch the boats go by.
audio/g7/s/this-is-la-moisson-the-harves: This is la moisson, the harvest, the busiest time of the farm year. Gold dust floats everywhere, and I sneezed twice.
audio/g7/s/this-is-the-alberta-badlands-: This is the Alberta badlands, beside the Red Deer River near the town of Drumheller. It is the traditional territory of the Blackfoot, the Nee-tsee-tah-pee. You say it nee-tsee-tah-pee.
audio/g7/s/this-is-the-prairie-of-southe: This is the prairie of southern Saskatchewan. The grass rolls away in every direction, gold and green, under a sky so big it seems to have no edge. In French it is la prairie, a word we borrowed.
audio/g7/s/this-is-treaty-6-and-treaty-7: This is Treaty 6 and Treaty 7 land. Plains First Nations have lived here for thousands of years, and still do. After the 1870s treaties it was opened to settlers, and First Nations families were pushed onto reserves.
audio/g7/s/this-is-where-i-say-thank-you: This is where I say thank you. Thank you, Zoe, Kai, Jade, Tyson, Priya and Lukas. You each showed me your home, and I will remember every one.
audio/g7/s/this-is-zoe-and-she-lives-rig: This is Zoe, and she lives right here in Thunder Bay. She says the lake is so cold in July that even the fish wear scarves.
audio/g7/s/through-the-window-we-can-rid: Through the window we can ride with a crew. Which canoe shall we climb into?
audio/g7/s/time-to-pay-at-the-post-you-c: Time to pay at the post you chose. Three right answers finishes our visit to The Forks.
audio/g7/s/to-trade-is-changer-in-french: To trade is échanger in French. I tried to trade a feather for a kettle. The clerk said it was a very nice feather, but no.
audio/g7/s/today-most-grain-is-kept-in-r: Today most grain is kept in round steel bins, which the French call le silo. They are cylinders with cone roofs, and they make a very good volume puzzle.
audio/g7/s/toot-toot-dot-has-grain-cars-: Toot toot! Dot has grain cars to pull, and she offers me a ride west into wheat country. Her cap nearly flew off when she waved, and she caught it with her tail.
audio/g7/s/treaty-6-was-made-in-1876-and: Treaty 6 was made in 1876 and Treaty 7 in 1877, between the Crown and the Cree, Nakoda, Blackfoot and other nations. The First Nations understood they were agreeing to share the land.
audio/g7/s/tyson-has-a-few-sharing-puzzl: Tyson has a few sharing puzzles about the camp and the grassland. Three right answers and the window opens again, and this time it is a hard look.
audio/g7/s/tyson-has-some-last-puzzles-f: Tyson has some last puzzles from the afternoon. Three right answers and we say goodbye.
audio/g7/s/tyson-is-quiet-too-then-he-sm: Tyson is quiet too. Then he smiles a little and says the story is not over, because the bison are back. He has two ideas for the afternoon. Shall we go out with the park rangers to count the herd, or walk with his auntie to look at the plants and the old tipi rings?
audio/g7/s/tyson-s-auntie-walks-us-over-: Tyson's auntie walks us over the hill, showing us the grasses and little flowers. Then she stops at a ring of stones lying in the grass. It is an old tipi ring, and the stones once held down the edges of a tipi.
audio/g7/s/tyson-says-many-nations-call-: Tyson says many nations call the plains home. They are the Nay-hee-yuh-wuk (Plains Cree), the Nakoda, the Nee-tsee-tah-pee (Blackfoot), the Dakota and Lakota, and the Soh-toh.
audio/g7/s/up-the-ladder-and-into-the-ca: Up the ladder and into the cab of the combine harvester with Lukas's mom! It cuts the wheat, shakes out the grain and drops the straw out the back, all in one pass. The seat is very high.
audio/g7/s/we-climb-into-a-big-canot-du-: We climb into a big canot du maître, about 11 metres long, with a crew of about 10 and roughly 60 pièces packed in. It rides low and steady across the open lake.
audio/g7/s/we-cross-to-the-north-west-co: We cross to the North West Company post, whose traders came from Montreal. The price list in Made Beaver says a gun is 16, a blanket is 10 and a kettle is 5.
audio/g7/s/we-hop-into-a-smaller-canot-d: We hop into a smaller canot du nord, with a crew of about 5 and roughly 25 pièces. It slips up the river, until we meet rapids that no one can paddle.
audio/g7/s/we-rolled-west-until-a-jagged: We rolled west until a jagged white line rose along the edge of the sky. Those are the Rocky Mountains, still far away, but tall enough to see from here.
audio/g7/s/we-step-into-the-hudson-s-bay: We step into the Hudson's Bay Company post. Wool blankets are stacked on the shelves and a clerk shows us the price list in Made Beaver. A gun is 20, a blanket is 8 and a kettle is 4.
audio/g7/s/we-walk-back-as-the-sun-sinks: We walk back as the sun sinks and the whole prairie glows. The bison are back on this land. The herd is small next to 30 million, but it is growing, and Tyson says that matters.
audio/g7/s/weather-is-a-farmer-s-biggest: Weather is a farmer's biggest worry, so let's work with chances and numbers. Three right answers and we pick a ride.
audio/g7/s/westward-ho-we-left-the-sea-o: Westward ho! We left the sea of grass behind, and now the ground below is striped. Grey, brown and rust red, like a giant cake that someone sliced.
audio/g7/s/when-a-dinosaur-died-mud-or-s: When a dinosaur died, mud or sand could bury it quickly. Over millions of years, minerals slowly replaced the bone and turned it to stone. That is a fossil, or le fossile.
audio/g7/s/when-a-train-came-the-grain-p: When a train came, the grain poured down a chute into the rail cars. The railway carried it to ports on the Pacific and the Great Lakes, and ships took it around the world.
audio/g7/s/when-the-bison-were-gone-the-: When the bison were gone, the Plains nations were starving. Canada's government used that hunger. It held back food until nations signed treaties and moved onto reserves.
audio/g7/s/when-the-hunt-was-ready-the-c: When the hunt was ready, the carts rolled west, squealing, out onto the open plains. There the grass goes on like a sea, and the great herds of le bison were waiting.
audio/g7/s/winters-were-brutal-and-the-n: Winters were brutal, and the nearest neighbour could be kilometres away. Lukas's great-great-grandparents began like this.
audio/g7/s/work-out-some-round-shapes-an: Work out some round shapes and a river lot. Three right answers and the window opens again.
audio/g7/s/work-out-the-speed-of-the-bri: Work out the speed of the brigades. Each right answer also earns you a Made Beaver, the fur trade money. Three right answers and we meet the canoe up close.
audio/g7/s/you-say-ah-nish-ih-nah-bay-li: You say Ah-nish-ih-nah-bay like this: ah-nish-ih-nah-bay.
audio/g7/s/you-say-may-tee-like-this-may: You say May-tee like this: may-tee.
audio/g7/s/you-say-mee-gwetch-like-this-: You say mee-gwetch like this: mee-gwetch. You say Ah-nish-ih-nah-bay-moh-win like this: ah-nish-ih-nah-bay-moh-win.
audio/g7/s/you-say-nakoda-like-this-nah-: You say Nakoda like this: nah-koh-dah.
audio/g7/s/you-say-nay-hee-yuh-wuk-like-: You say Nay-hee-yuh-wuk like this: nay-hee-yuh-wuk. Nee-tsee-tah-pee is nee-tsee-tah-pee. Soh-toh is soh-toh.
audio/g7/s/zoe-tells-me-the-ah-nish-ih-n: Zoe tells me the Ah-nish-ih-nah-bay, who are also called the Ojibwe, have lived around this lake since long before there was any fort. Fort William First Nation is right beside the city today.
audio/g8/s/a-canoe-is-le-canot-in-french: A canoe is le canot in French. Everyone paddles together, and Kayla's family sets the pace.
audio/g8/s/a-case-file-in-three-steps-di: A case file in three steps: did a gold miner of 1858 end up ahead or behind? Three right answers, one step at a time, and then you choose how we spend the afternoon.
audio/g8/s/a-certificate-is-waiting-for-: A certificate is waiting for you. Hang it on the wall, or on the fridge, or both. And thank you. I mean it with every feather.
audio/g8/s/a-last-set-of-problems-from-o: A last set of problems from our time on the harbour. Three right answers and we say goodbye.
audio/g8/s/a-river-is-la-rivi-re-in-fren: A river is la rivière in French. I am looking for a boy who knows this river better than anyone. I think I will land on that gravel bank.
audio/g8/s/a-ship-is-le-navire-in-french: A ship is le navire in French. We stand there quietly for a while, and nobody feels like talking.
audio/g8/s/a-tiny-heap-of-dust-goes-onto: A tiny heap of dust goes onto a little set of scales, la balance in French. Gold is sold by its mass, so the scales matter a great deal.
audio/g8/s/a-train-cannot-climb-a-steep-: A train cannot climb a steep slope, so the track has to rise slowly. Three right answers and we look at the rails today.
audio/g8/s/a-tunnel-is-le-tunnel-in-fren: A tunnel is le tunnel in French. Mei says that the first builders of this railway worked on mountains like these with hand tools and explosives, and she is quiet for a while as we ride.
audio/g8/s/afraid-that-their-songs-and-d: Afraid that their songs and dances will be lost in all the upheaval, he sends them to relatives in Alaska for safekeeping. Generations later, they are brought home.
audio/g8/s/after-that-the-land-is-wide-f: After that the land is wide, flat and open. This is Nunavut. By my pocket watch it is nearly midnight, and the sky is still bright! In summer here the sun dips down for only a little while, and it never gets dark.
audio/g8/s/along-the-way-mei-points-up-a: Along the way Mei points up at a railway bridge high over a creek. A bridge is le pont in French. Mei says she has walked this trail many times, and she still stops at the cairn to read the plaque.
audio/g8/s/and-last-that-every-place-had: And last, that every place had a child who knew it better than any book. Lily nods slowly. She says that will do very nicely.
audio/g8/s/and-last-the-friends-from-the: And last the friends from the mountains and the North, Grade 8: Mei, Jordan, Simran, Kayla, Hannah and Dana. That is twenty-two friends on one riverbank, and one very proud owl in the middle.
audio/g8/s/and-there-is-the-grand-river-: And there is the Grand River, winding silver below, and the bridge at Brantford, and a small figure on the bank. It is Lily, from Six Nations of the Grand River. She is standing on the very same bank where my story began.
audio/g8/s/back-in-the-present-dana-is-q: Back in the present, Dana is quiet for a moment. She tells us the Tron-dek Hwitch-in are still here, and in 1998 they signed a modern land claim and self-government agreement. Then she smiles. Cam has driven up to meet us, with two ideas for the afternoon. Shall we climb a stretch of the Chilkoot Trail, or pan for gold at a creek claim?
audio/g8/s/back-in-the-present-nina-walk: Back in the present, Nina walks me through town. The houses are painted red, yellow and blue, and they stand on stilts, tall legs that lift them off the ground. One of them is leaning a little. I lean too, to see how it feels.
audio/g8/s/back-in-today-jordan-walks-us: Back in today! Jordan walks us to the water's edge. The Fraser rolls on past Hope, and the salmon keep swimming against the current, just as they have for thousands of years.
audio/g8/s/back-in-today-kayla-tells-us-: Back in today, Kayla tells us a hard part of the story, and I listen. From 1885 to 1951, which is 66 years, Canada's law made the potlatch a crime. A law is la loi in French.
audio/g8/s/back-to-today-mei-takes-us-up: Back to today! Mei takes us up to the Kicking Horse Pass. A loaded train cannot climb steeply, so a railway is built to a gentle grade, about 2.2 metres up for every 100 metres along.
audio/g8/s/back-to-today-this-is-a-count: Back to today! This is a counting station on the Fraser. Sockeye salmon are swimming upriver, and people count every fish that passes the fence. A salmon is le saumon.
audio/g8/s/below-us-is-vancouver-in-brit: Below us is Vancouver, in British Columbia. Mountains with snowy tops stand behind the city, and a long blue inlet runs in front of it.
audio/g8/s/cam-and-dana-have-some-last-p: Cam and Dana have some last puzzles from the afternoon. Three right answers and we say goodbye.
audio/g8/s/cam-leads-us-up-a-stretch-of-: Cam leads us up a stretch of the Chilkoot Trail, one careful step at a time. A narrow path like this is a trail, le sentier in French. I counted my steps, and then I lost count of my counting.
audio/g8/s/cam-says-every-hiker-today-wa: Cam says every hiker today walks the same ground as the Klink-it traders, the packers and the gold seekers before them. We stop often to look back at how far we have climbed.
audio/g8/s/cedar-planks-great-logs-and-s: Cedar planks, great logs and shipping containers are all solid shapes. Three right answers and we come back to the city today.
audio/g8/s/container-ships-wait-on-the-w: Container ships wait on the water, and seaplanes buzz in and out like dragonflies. A place where ships come and go is le port, the harbour. This one is Burrard Inlet.
audio/g8/s/counting-fish-and-following-t: Counting fish and following their swim on a graph. Three right answers and we look at the river today.
audio/g8/s/counting-matters-because-some: Counting matters because some years the run is tiny. In 1913 and 1914, blasting for the railway sent rock sliding into the canyon at Hells Gate and blocked the river. The run collapsed.
audio/g8/s/dana-says-her-people-have-fis: Dana says her people have fished and hunted along these rivers for thousands of years. The tall wooden false-front buildings around us are more than a hundred years old.
audio/g8/s/dana-shows-us-how-to-pan-you-: Dana shows us how to pan. You scoop gravel and water into the pan and swirl it round and round. The heavy gold sinks, and the light gravel washes away. I mostly got wet.
audio/g8/s/down-in-the-valley-a-long-tra: Down in the valley a long train is climbing the grade. Freight trains still haul goods through these passes every day. Why is there a railway in such steep mountains? Let us find out.
audio/g8/s/every-morning-someone-writes-: Every morning someone writes down the temperature, and now there is a long list of numbers to work with. The weather in French is la météo. I am in charge of the pencil. Nina is in charge of me.
audio/g8/s/every-one-of-them-is-a-place-: Every one of them is a place I visited, and every one had somebody waiting. It was a very long way round. It turns out it is also a short way home.
audio/g8/s/families-also-hold-great-gath: Families also hold great gatherings, which outsiders later called the potlatch. A host feeds the guests for days and gives away wealth. Giving, not keeping, shows a family's standing.
audio/g8/s/families-kept-their-gathering: Families kept their gatherings going in secret. Since 1951 they have been held openly again, and some of the things that were taken have been returned.
audio/g8/s/families-stand-on-rock-ledges: Families stand on rock ledges over the rushing water and lift salmon out with long dip nets. A net is le filet in French. Each fishing place is looked after by a family and handed down.
audio/g8/s/far-below-a-wide-river-is-rus: Far below, a wide river is rushing through the gap. This is the Fraser River, in British Columbia. Look at the water! Something red keeps leaping out of it.
audio/g8/s/far-below-two-rivers-meet-one: Far below, two rivers meet. One is wide and slow, the Yukon. The other is smaller and joins it, the Klondike. At the meeting place there is a small town of wooden buildings.
audio/g8/s/farther-north-the-sun-does-no: Farther north the sun does not set for weeks. In French that is le soleil de minuit, the midnight sun. Even here my owl eyes cannot decide whether to sleep. And somebody on the shore is waving at us.
audio/g8/s/first-that-this-country-is-ma: First, that this country is many peoples' home. Everywhere I went, someone's family had been there for a very long time, and other families had come and made a home too.
audio/g8/s/fishways-were-built-later-so-: Fishways were built later so that fish could get past. Warmer water and too much fishing hurt the salmon too, so people keep counting and keep watching.
audio/g8/s/gold-seekers-pour-in-by-the-t: Gold seekers pour in by the thousands, and people build a new town. Government officials let them take the land. The Tron-dek Hwitch-in are pushed out of their camp.
audio/g8/s/goodbye-jordan-and-goodbye-sa: Goodbye, Jordan, and goodbye, salmon! The Fraser River has carried us down out of the mountains, and now the water is wide and salty and the air smells of the sea.
audio/g8/s/goodbye-mei-and-goodbye-railw: Goodbye, Mei, and goodbye, railway! My clock balloon has floated down out of the Rocky Mountains, and now I am drifting between two steep walls of rock.
audio/g8/s/higher-up-in-the-canyon-is-th: Higher up in the canyon is the land of the Ing-kla-kap-muh people. You say it ing-kla-kap-muh. Every year the salmon swim past all of them. Jordan says to look through the clock and see how his family fished long ago.
audio/g8/s/i-found-a-flake-it-was-so-sma: I found a flake! It was so small I almost sneezed it back into the river. Keep still, Dr. Somebody.
audio/g8/s/i-go-quiet-and-so-does-nina-t: I go quiet, and so does Nina. Then she says that her people are still here, and the bowhead whales are still here too. We look at some numbers, because numbers help us see what is happening now.
audio/g8/s/i-land-the-balloon-as-gently-: I land the balloon as gently as an owl can, which is to say with a bump and a hoot. Then I sit down beside her on the grass, because it is a good question and it needs sitting down for.
audio/g8/s/i-talk-for-a-whole-minute-wit: I talk for a whole minute without stopping. Nina waits politely until I finish. Then she says, You still talk too much, Dr. Somebody. She is right. I am very pleased to see her anyway.
audio/g8/s/in-1923-a-new-law-shut-out-al: In 1923 a new law shut out almost all Chinese immigration. It stayed until 1947. Families were kept apart for decades, a husband in Canada and a wife and children in China.
audio/g8/s/in-2006-the-government-of-can: In 2006 the government of Canada formally apologized. Mei's family is here today, and she tells this story so that it is remembered. Now, the numbers. They are worth looking at carefully.
audio/g8/s/in-2016-the-prime-minister-of: In 2016 the Prime Minister of Canada stood in Parliament and apologized for what was done to the people on that ship.
audio/g8/s/in-the-klondike-gold-dust-was: In the Klondike, gold dust was money, and money has to be weighed and counted. Three right answers and the window opens again, and this time it is a serious look.
audio/g8/s/it-is-called-every-child-matt: It is called Every Child Matters. Tick tock!
audio/g8/s/it-is-nina-last-time-i-saw-he: It is Nina! Last time I saw her it was dark winter, and she showed me the ig-loo, the koo-lik and the kah-moo-teek. She is a few years older now and taller too. I am so delighted I jump up and down.
audio/g8/s/it-was-your-answers-that-open: It was your answers that opened every door. Every chime, every window, every gate on this long trip, you found the key. I only drove the balloon, and not always in a straight line.
audio/g8/s/jordan-has-two-ideas-for-the-: Jordan has two ideas for the afternoon. We could go out with the fish counters at the counting fence, or pan for gold at a sandbar with his uncle. People still do, for fun, and find a few flakes. Which one?
audio/g8/s/jordan-lets-me-try-click-clic: Jordan lets me try. Click, click, click! It is much harder than it looks, because the fish do not wait in a line, and one of them splashed my feathers.
audio/g8/s/jordan-s-uncle-takes-us-to-a-: Jordan's uncle takes us to a gravel bar and shows us how to swirl the pan so the heavy flakes sink. People still pan here for fun, and with luck you find a few tiny flakes. A lump of gold is la pépite, a nugget.
audio/g8/s/jordan-says-his-people-have-w: Jordan says his people have watched this river through everything that has happened, the gold rush, the colony and the sickness. They are still here, still fishing, and still looking after it.
audio/g8/s/kayla-s-family-invites-us-int: Kayla's family invites us into a long cedar canoe, and we paddle out onto the inlet in life jackets. Canoe journeys are held today, and the mountains slide slowly past.
audio/g8/s/la-montagne-is-the-french-wor: La montagne is the French word for a mountain, and these are very big ones. The peaks are sharp and white at the top, and the slopes below are dark with evergreen trees. This is the land of the Suh-wep-muhc, the K-too-nah-ha, the Sin-aykst and other nations, who live here today.
audio/g8/s/look-at-the-picture-the-track: Look at the picture. The track goes into the mountain, circles inside it and comes out higher up. A long freight train can be at both ends of a loop at the same time.
audio/g8/s/mei-has-one-more-set-of-quest: Mei has one more set of questions about the way we chose. Three right answers and we say goodbye to the mountains.
audio/g8/s/mei-has-two-places-to-show-us: Mei has two places to show us. We can ride a train through the Spiral Tunnels, or walk the trail to the cairn at Kray-gell-uh-kee where the last spike was driven. Which shall we do?
audio/g8/s/mei-s-great-great-great-grand: Mei's great-great-great-grandfather came from Guangdong, in southern China, to help build this railway. In Cantonese a railway is teet-loh, and Mei says the word slowly and carefully.
audio/g8/s/mei-wants-us-to-see-one-day-i: Mei wants us to see one day in particular, November 7, 1885. But first we must see how the railway got here. Clock, show us!
audio/g8/s/na-koor-meek-nina-for-the-ig-: Na-koor-meek, Nina, for the ig-loo in winter, the ice in summer, and for telling it plainly. The balloon rises over the flowers and the floes. Next we go Home. Tick tock!
audio/g8/s/next-the-clock-turns-inland-t: Next the clock turns inland, to the dry hills of the interior. There is a story there that every child in Canada should hear. I will listen more than I talk.
audio/g8/s/next-we-follow-the-rails-down: Next we follow the rails down the canyon to a river with its own story of gold. It is called the Fraser, and the chapter is The River of Gold. Tick tock!
audio/g8/s/nina-has-some-graphs-to-read-: Nina has some graphs to read. They are made-up examples, but they show the kind of trend scientists look for. Three right answers opens the window again.
audio/g8/s/nina-has-some-last-puzzles-fr: Nina has some last puzzles from our adventure. Three right answers and we say goodbye.
audio/g8/s/nina-has-some-temperature-puz: Nina has some temperature puzzles from her winter notebook, with a lot of minus signs. Three right answers and we go for a walk through her town. Each right answer also earns you a piece of gold dust.
audio/g8/s/nina-s-class-keeps-a-small-we: Nina's class keeps a small weather station outside the school. It is a white box with slats on four legs, and a wind vane on a pole. The slats let the air in and keep the sun off the thermometer.
audio/g8/s/nina-s-uncle-and-the-elders-h: Nina's uncle and the elders have watched all of this for decades. Scientists now work with them, because what Ih-noo-it know goes back much further than any instrument. Nina says it is time to look at some data.
audio/g8/s/nina-s-uncle-has-a-puzzle-abo: Nina's uncle has a puzzle about the sea ice. This is a case file with three steps, and each step uses the answer from the one before. Three right answers in a row solve the case.
audio/g8/s/nina-s-uncle-knows-this-ice-w: Nina's uncle knows this ice well. He tests it carefully before every step, and we follow exactly in his footsteps. He pushes a long pole down through a small hole and reads the thickness in centimetres.
audio/g8/s/nina-says-that-now-the-people: Nina says that now the people who live in Nunavut make the big decisions about their own land. Everyone in the picture is dancing. I ask if there is cake. There is always cake.
audio/g8/s/nina-says-the-next-place-i-sh: Nina says the next place I should go is home. The clock agrees. Its hand swings round to the south and east, all the way back to where the journey began, the Grand River. Nina says I can visit again, but I must talk less.
audio/g8/s/nine-hundred-kilograms-is-a-l: Nine hundred kilograms is a lot to carry up a mountain. Three right answers and the clock hops us to the Chilkoot Pass. Each right answer also earns you a pinch of gold dust.
audio/g8/s/no-treaties-were-made-for-alm: No treaties were made for almost all of this land. It was never sold or given up, and that is still being worked out today, in courts and in new agreements.
audio/g8/s/now-ships-come-north-from-bri: Now ships come north from Britain and America each summer, looking for bowhead whales. Traders follow them, looking for fox furs. Ih-noo-it work with the newcomers as hunters and guides, and they sew warm clothing.
audio/g8/s/nunavut-has-a-public-governme: Nunavut has a public government, one that serves everyone who lives there. Most of the people of Nunavut are Ih-noo-it, so Ih-noo-it lead it.
audio/g8/s/on-a-wooden-boardwalk-a-girl-: On a wooden boardwalk a girl is waiting for us. This is Dana. She lives in Dawson, and she is a citizen of the Tron-dek Hwitch-in, the First Nation whose land this is.
audio/g8/s/on-april-1-1999-nunavut-becam: On April 1, 1999, Nunavut became Canada's newest territory. Nunavut means our land in Ih-nook-tih-toot. Ih-nook-tih-toot is one of its official languages.
audio/g8/s/out-with-the-old-in-with-the-: Out with the old, in with the new! It's been a hoooot!
audio/g8/s/people-come-from-all-over-the: People come from all over the world to hear about the gold. We already know the French word for gold, l'or. I held a gold coin once, and I gave it back, because it was heavier than it looked.
audio/g8/s/people-were-arrested-and-jail: People were arrested and jailed. Masks, blankets and other treasures were taken from families and sent to museums.
audio/g8/s/second-that-the-people-who-we: Second, that the people who were here first are still here. Not in a museum. Here, now, in their own towns and cities, speaking, teaching and laughing at my jokes. Mostly laughing.
audio/g8/s/she-adds-that-this-land-was-n: She adds that this land was never given up by treaty. Her best friend Kayla is from the Squamish Nation, and Kayla wants to show us the cedar. Clock, show us!
audio/g8/s/she-greets-us-with-sut-sree-u: She greets us with sut sree uh-kaal, a Sikh greeting, and I say it back as well as an owl can. You say it sut sree uh-kaal.
audio/g8/s/she-is-older-now-and-taller-a: She is older now, and taller, and so, I suppose, am I. She says Nyah-wen, thank you for coming back. Then she folds her arms and asks the question I knew was coming. What did you learn?
audio/g8/s/simran-and-kayla-each-have-so: Simran and Kayla each have somewhere to take us. Shall we paddle with Kayla's family in a cedar canoe on the inlet, or visit the memorial with Simran's grandfather?
audio/g8/s/simran-listens-too-and-says-n: Simran listens too, and says nothing for a while. Then she says there is another story on this same harbour, about another law, and she wants us to hear it.
audio/g8/s/simran-s-family-is-here-today: Simran's family is here today, and a memorial to the Komagata Maru stands on the harbour. Simran says the ship waited two months with its water running out. That is a problem we can look at plainly.
audio/g8/s/simran-s-grandfather-meets-us: Simran's grandfather meets us at the waterfront. He walks us to the memorial to the Komagata Maru, which stands on the harbour and looks out over the water where the ship waited.
audio/g8/s/simran-tells-us-this-city-sta: Simran tells us this city stands on the land of three Coast Salish nations, the Mus-kwee-um, the Squamish and the Slay-wah-tuth. They have lived here for thousands of years, and they live here today.
audio/g8/s/six-friends-have-each-sent-on: Six friends have each sent one last question, one from every part of the journey. Six right answers and they will all come to say hello.
audio/g8/s/sockeye-swim-hundreds-of-kilo: Sockeye swim hundreds of kilometres up the river to lay their eggs where they were born. On the way their bodies turn red and their heads turn green.
audio/g8/s/some-of-these-numbers-are-ver: Some of these numbers are very big. Three right answers and the window opens on the spring of 1858, where two people will tell us what they see.
audio/g8/s/some-people-dragged-their-goo: Some people dragged their goods on a sled, le traîneau, where the ground was gentler. Money was a worry too. Gold dust was weighed on scales to pay bills, and some people borrowed from outfitters and paid interest.
audio/g8/s/some-plain-numbers-now-three-: Some plain numbers now. Three right answers and the window opens on the summer of 1914.
audio/g8/s/staw-low-means-people-of-the-: Staw-low means people of the river, in Halk-uh-may-lem (say halk-uh-may-lem), the language of his people. Jordan says the name tells you everything. The river is home and food, all in one.
audio/g8/s/thank-you-dana-and-thank-you-: Thank you, Dana, and thank you, Cam. Now the clock turns north, past the last of the trees, to the top of the world. An old friend is waiting there, and I think you know her. It is The Top of the World, in Nunavut, where Nina lives. Tick tock!
audio/g8/s/thank-you-jordan-next-we-foll: Thank you, Jordan! Next we follow the river down to the sea, in The Harbour and the Cedar. Tick tock!
audio/g8/s/thank-you-mei-he-was-not-in-t: Thank you, Mei. He was not in the photograph, but you keep his story, and now we do too.
audio/g8/s/the-arctic-is-warming-about-t: The Arctic is warming about three to four times faster than the rest of the world. The sea ice forms later in the fall and breaks up earlier in the spring. That makes travelling and hunting on it less safe. Animals are changing where they go too.
audio/g8/s/the-canadian-pacific-railway-: The Canadian Pacific Railway is building it, and the hardest part is here, through these mountains and the Fraser Canyon. About 15,000 Chinese workers came to build the British Columbia section.
audio/g8/s/the-clock-hops-us-south-over-: The clock hops us south, over the mountains, to the foot of the Chilkoot Pass. Dana's cousin Cam is here, a trail guide in an orange vest. Above us a line of tiny figures climbs a steep white slope.
audio/g8/s/the-clock-is-quiet-and-so-am-: The clock is quiet, and so am I. Here is what came next, plainly. In 1858, Britain made the mainland a colony, British Columbia, to keep control of the gold fields.
audio/g8/s/the-clock-is-quiet-this-morni: The clock is quiet this morning, and so am I. We drift north over mountains and then over a long, wide valley with low wooded hills. The air is clear and cool.
audio/g8/s/the-clock-points-north-and-th: The clock points north and the balloon climbs. We leave the Klondike and the gold rush behind. We cross the Northwest Territories, and then we pass the tree line, where it is too cold for trees to grow.
audio/g8/s/the-clock-points-south-and-ea: The clock points south and east, and for once I let it pull. Below us the Arctic tundra slides by, flat and wide and dotted with a thousand little lakes. Nina is still waving somewhere behind.
audio/g8/s/the-coast-salish-peoples-buil: The Coast Salish peoples build great houses of long cedar planks, with low sloped roofs. They carve canoes from single cedar logs. They weave cedar bark into clothing, rope and baskets, and they weave blankets too.
audio/g8/s/the-first-track-over-this-pas: The first track over this pass, the Big Hill, rose 4.5 percent, which was dangerously steep. In 1909 the Spiral Tunnels opened: two loops inside the mountains that let the track rise slowly.
audio/g8/s/the-fish-are-split-open-and-h: The fish are split open and hung on racks in the warm, dry wind of the canyon. Dried salmon lasts all winter, with plenty left over to trade.
audio/g8/s/the-ground-under-the-town-is-: The ground under the town is frozen all year. It is called permafrost, le pergélisol in French. Now the permafrost is thawing, so the ground shifts, and buildings and roads can tilt and crack.
audio/g8/s/the-guests-are-the-witnesses-: The guests are the witnesses. They watch, and they remember what was done. Kayla says gatherings are held today too. Now for some solid shapes.
audio/g8/s/the-last-climb-was-so-steep-t: The last climb was so steep that 1,500 steps were cut into the ice and snow. People called them the Golden Stairs. One person could carry only 25 to 30 kilograms at a time, so a ton took 30 or 40 trips, up and back down, for weeks.
audio/g8/s/the-last-puzzle-of-all-is-a-c: The last puzzle of all is a case file in three steps, about the whole journey. The numbers are rough and round. Three right answers and I have something to tell you.
audio/g8/s/the-mountainside-is-full-of-r: The mountainside is full of right triangles. Three right answers and the window opens on one day in 1885.
audio/g8/s/the-news-reaches-the-outside-: The news reaches the outside world in 1897, and about 100,000 people set out for the Klondike. This is the gold rush, la ruée vers l'or. Only about 30,000 to 40,000 arrive, and only a few thousand find any gold.
audio/g8/s/the-north-west-mounted-police: The North-West Mounted Police will not let anyone into the Yukon without a year of supplies, about a ton (roughly 900 kilograms), so that nobody starves. One way in is over the Chilkoot Pass, on foot.
audio/g8/s/the-numbers-tell-him-whether-: The numbers tell him whether the ice can be trusted, and where it can be crossed. Ice in French is la glace. I keep my wings out for balance. Nina says I look like a very nervous airplane.
audio/g8/s/the-others-have-said-goodnigh: The others have said goodnight and gone home along the river. It is very quiet. I hang my goggles on the basket, and I say it out loud to the stars. I am home for good. I find that I mean it.
audio/g8/s/the-potlatch-law-tried-to-era: The potlatch law tried to erase the ways of people who had always belonged here. The rule against the Komagata Maru shut the door on newcomers before they could step ashore.
audio/g8/s/the-prairie-is-behind-us-and-: The prairie is behind us, and look at what the clock was pointing at! My balloon is climbing into the Rocky Mountains of British Columbia. My ears have popped three times already.
audio/g8/s/the-river-does-not-stop-here-: The river does not stop here. It runs out across a wide flat delta and into the sea, near a great harbour. A big city has grown up there, with an old, old story under its cedar trees.
audio/g8/s/the-sky-is-still-bright-and-i: The sky is still bright, and I realize that I have been here a whole day without noticing. This is the farthest north the balloon will go. At the top of the world, every direction points south.

The sky is still bright, and it is time to choose. Nina's uncle is going out on the sea ice to check how thick it is with a long measuring pole, and we are invited. Or we could help Nina's class with the weather station outside the school. Which shall it be?
audio/g8/s/the-staw-low-and-the-ing-kla-: The Staw-low and the Ing-kla-kap-muh are still here, and so is the river. Jordan's family still fishes it.
audio/g8/s/the-sun-is-going-down-behind-: The sun is going down behind the peaks, and the rails run on, across a high wooden bridge and down the canyon of a great river, toward the sea.
The sun is going down behind the mountains, and the lights of the ships are coming on. Simran and Kayla stand side by side.
audio/g8/s/the-tron-dek-hwitch-in-are-st: The Tron-dek Hwitch-in are still here, where the Klondike meets the Yukon, and Dana is growing up on this land. The gold rush lasted a few years. The river and the people have been here far longer.
audio/g8/s/the-tron-dek-hwitch-in-had-fi: The Tron-dek Hwitch-in had fished and hunted here for thousands of years. Their camp was at Troh-chek. You say it troh-chek.
audio/g8/s/the-window-again-and-this-tim: The window again, and this time it is 1999. Ih-noo-it leaders worked for many years for this. The Nunavut land claim was signed in 1993, and now a whole territory is celebrating. Nina's grandmother remembers this day.
audio/g8/s/the-window-closes-and-i-am-qu: The window closes, and I am quiet for a while. Then Simran tells me the rest. When the ship reached India, police tried to arrest the passengers at a place called Budge Budge. About 20 of them were shot and killed.
The window closes, and I am quiet for a while. Here is what came next, plainly. The head tax was raised to 100 dollars in 1900, and to 500 dollars in 1903. That was about two years of wages.
audio/g8/s/the-window-into-the-past-it-i: The window into the past! It is August 1896, at Rabbit Creek, soon to be renamed Bonanza Creek. A small party is here: Kaysh, called Skookum Jim, and his sister Shaw Tlah, called Kate Carmack.

The window into the past! It is about 1850. For thousands of years Ih-noo-it have lived here by their own knowledge of the ice, the animals and the weather. They know where the whales swim and when the ice can be trusted.
The window into the past! It is the early 1880s. British Columbia joined Canada in 1871 on the promise of a railway to the Pacific. A railway is le chemin de fer in French.
audio/g8/s/the-window-into-the-past-long: The window into the past! Long before the city, this shore is thick with giant trees. Kayla points at the biggest. It is a cedar, le cèdre in French.
audio/g8/s/the-window-into-the-past-we-a: The window into the past! We are looking back long before 1858, long before any railway or town. The river runs deep and fast through the canyon, and the salmon are coming home.
audio/g8/s/the-window-opens-again-and-i-: The window opens again, and I go quiet. It is 1898. In two years a fish camp at the river mouth has become a city of about 30,000 people. For a moment it is one of the largest cities in western Canada.
audio/g8/s/their-leader-chief-isaac-move: Their leader, Chief Isaac, moves his people a few kilometres downriver to Moosehide, to keep them together.
audio/g8/s/then-in-1862-smallpox-came-up: Then, in 1862, smallpox came up the coast and through the province. It killed tens of thousands of First Nations people, and some communities lost more than half of their people in a single year.
audio/g8/s/then-the-clock-begins-to-spin: Then the clock begins to spin, faster than it has ever spun before. Its hands become a blur, lines of light spinning out into the dark. It points at nowhere on any map. I look at it. I look at you.
audio/g8/s/then-the-clock-on-the-balloon: Then the clock on the balloon begins to chime, soft and clear, one note after another. Along the riverbank the friends appear one by one, as if the notes had called them. First the Grade 5 friends: Lily, Noah, Maya and Nina.
audio/g8/s/then-the-friends-from-the-eas: Then the friends from the east, Grade 6: Léa, Olivier, Élodie, Sadie, Amara and Declan. Léa waves with both arms, and the notes keep coming.
audio/g8/s/then-the-friends-from-the-wes: Then the friends from the west, Grade 7: Zoe, Kai, Jade, Tyson, Priya and Lukas. They walk across the grass as if they had only been over the next hill.
audio/g8/s/then-the-prairies-a-quilt-of-: Then the prairies, a quilt of gold and green. Then the forest, and the rock, and the Great Lakes, so big they look like seas. I name every place out loud as it passes, the way you say goodnight to people you love.
audio/g8/s/there-are-two-stories-on-one-: There are two stories on one harbour, the cedar and the ship. Both are about laws that told people they did not belong, and both are told today by the people who carry them. Thank you, Simran and Kayla.
audio/g8/s/there-is-one-more-thank-you-a: There is one more thank you, and it is for you. Yes, you, the one reading this. You are the child who has been travelling with me all this time.
audio/g8/s/they-also-had-to-buy-their-ow: They also had to buy their own food and gear out of that pay. Hundreds died in rock slides, blasts and accidents and from illness. At least 600 is the number most often given.
audio/g8/s/they-were-given-the-most-dang: They were given the most dangerous jobs, like handling explosives to blast tunnels and ledges out of the rock. They were paid about one dollar a day, roughly half of what white workers were paid.
audio/g8/s/third-that-some-of-our-histor: Third, that some of our history is hard, and that telling it truthfully is how you look after a place. You cannot mend what you will not look at.
audio/g8/s/this-is-a-case-file-one-probl: This is a case file: one problem in three steps, and each answer feeds the next. Cam is packing a ton for a stampeder. Three right answers and we choose how to spend the afternoon.
audio/g8/s/this-is-a-case-file-three-ste: This is a case file: three steps about one worker's pay, and each answer is used in the next. Three right answers and we go on.
This is a case file, three steps about a real problem on the ship: the water. Each answer is used in the next step. Three right answers and we go on.
audio/g8/s/this-is-dawson-city-in-the-yu: This is Dawson City, in the Yukon. In summer the sun hardly sets here, and in winter it is deep cold. We land softly beside the river.
audio/g8/s/this-is-jordan-he-is-a-staw-l: This is Jordan. He is a Staw-low boy, and he lives near Hope, where the river comes out of the canyon. His family has fished this river for as long as anyone can remember.
audio/g8/s/this-is-mei-she-lives-in-reve: This is Mei. She lives in Revelstoke, a mountain town in British Columbia, and she can hear the freight trains from her bedroom window. She says she can tell which train is coming by the sound.
audio/g8/s/this-is-simran-she-lives-in-v: This is Simran. She lives in Vancouver, and she has come down to the water to meet us. Her family is Sikh, and her great-great-grandfather came here from Punjab, in India.
audio/g8/s/this-time-it-is-summer-the-op: This time it is summer, the opposite season. Flowers cover the tundra, and the ice in the bay is breaking up. Nina's home is far up in le nord, the north. Clock, show us what came before!
audio/g8/s/time-for-the-numbers-of-the-a: Time for the numbers of the afternoon you chose. Three right answers and we say goodbye to the river.
audio/g8/s/today-they-are-hikers-in-1898: Today they are hikers. In 1898 they were gold seekers. The Chilkoot Trail was a trading route of the Klink-it long before the gold rush, and Klink-it packers carried loads for the gold seekers.
audio/g8/s/we-climb-aboard-with-mei-and-: We climb aboard with Mei, and the train rumbles into the mountain. Inside it is dark and loud, and the track circles round until we come out higher up, with the same valley far below us.
audio/g8/s/we-pull-on-bright-orange-vest: We pull on bright orange vests and walk out to the fence with a fish counter. Each time a salmon swims through the gate, she clicks her counter once. To count is compter in French.
audio/g8/s/we-walk-back-to-the-boardwalk: We walk back to the boardwalk in the long evening light, and the sun is still up. Dana says in summer it hardly sets at all. I hope it does not mind me borrowing a little of it for my balloon.
audio/g8/s/we-walk-the-trail-to-kray-gel: We walk the trail to Kray-gell-uh-kee with Mei leading the way. At the end stands a stone cairn with a plaque that marks the place where the last spike was driven, and the tracks run right past it.
audio/g8/s/when-smallpox-reached-victori: When smallpox reached Victoria in 1862, the colony's officials forced the First Nations people camped there to leave, and the sickness travelled north along the coast with them.
audio/g8/s/with-them-are-their-nephew-ka: With them are their nephew Kah Gokh, called Dawson Charlie, and Kate's husband George Carmack. Kaysh, Shaw Tlah and Kah Gokh are Tagish and Klink-it. Together they find gold in the creek.
audio/g8/s/without-that-help-the-newcome: Without that help the newcomers could not have survived in the Arctic. But the whalers kill so many bowhead whales that almost none are left. They also bring sicknesses that Ih-noo-it have never met, and many people die.
audio/g8/s/you-say-mus-kwee-um-like-mus-: You say Mus-kwee-um like mus-kwee-um, and Slay-wah-tuth like slay-wah-tuth.
audio/g8/s/you-say-staw-low-like-this-st: You say Staw-low like this: staw-low.
audio/g8/s/you-say-them-suh-wep-muhc-k-t: You say them suh-wep-muhc, k-too-nah-ha and sin-aykst.
audio/g5/clock/tick-tock-tick-tock-i-hav: Tick, tock. Tick, tock. I have something to show you.
audio/g5/clock/tick-tock-time-to-look-ba: Tick, tock. Time to look back. My window is open.
audio/g6/clock/tick-tock-the-window-open: Tick, tock. The window opens again.
audio/g6/clock/tick-tock-time-to-look-ba: Tick, tock. Time to look back. My window is open.
audio/g7/clock/but-i-worry-the-beaver-ar: But I worry. The beaver are fewer every year. When too many are trapped, the lodges go quiet. What will the trade be when the beaver are gone?
audio/g7/clock/every-kettle-and-every-bl: Every kettle and every blanket on these shelves crossed the ocean by ship, then went inland by canoe and boat for weeks. That costs a great deal, so I think my prices are fair. I weigh each pelt honestly.
audio/g7/clock/i-am-a-cree-hunter-and-tr: I am a Cree hunter and trader. Each bundle of furs is a whole winter of skilled work. I trap in deep snow, I skin and stretch every pelt, and then I carry them many days to reach the post.
audio/g7/clock/i-am-a-nakoda-grandmother: I am a Nakoda grandmother of the plains. I remember when the ground shook with the herds, and the whole camp was fed. In my own lifetime I have watched them vanish. First the herds were smaller. Then they were gone.
audio/g7/clock/i-came-west-in-the-1870s-: I came west in the 1870s because a man could earn good money here. They pay me by the hide. On a good day I shoot dozens of bison with my big rifle.
audio/g7/clock/i-keep-the-books-at-this-: I keep the books at this post for the Hudson's Bay Company. Here we price everything in Made Beaver. One prime beaver pelt is 1 Made Beaver, and a gun, a kettle or a blanket each cost a set number of pelts.
audio/g7/clock/i-take-the-skins-and-i-le: I take the skins and I leave the rest on the ground. The hides go east by wagon and by rail, and the railway creeps further west every year. The land is being cleared for farms and ranches.
audio/g7/clock/i-tell-my-grandchildren-a: I tell my grandchildren all of this, so it is never forgotten. We are still here.
audio/g7/clock/nobody-forces-me-to-trade: Nobody forces me to trade at one post. Two companies want my furs, so I can choose the one with the better deal. The kettles and blankets really are useful, and a good kettle saves my family hours of work.
audio/g7/clock/the-herds-look-endless-to: The herds look endless to me. I think there are too many ever to be gone. I think about the money. Then one year I ride for days and cannot find a single herd.
audio/g7/clock/the-list-is-the-same-for-: The list is the same for every hunter who walks in. Both sides want the same thing, which is good goods in return for good fur.
audio/g7/clock/then-we-were-pressed-to-s: Then we were pressed to sign treaties and to move onto reserves, and we were promised food and help. Many of those promises were broken. Some people in power did not stop the killing.
audio/g7/clock/without-the-bison-hunger-: Without the bison, hunger came. Many of our people starved. We had lost our food, our shelter and our clothing all at once.
audio/g8/clock/canada-has-a-rule-immigra: Canada has a rule: immigrants must come by one continuous journey from their home country. No ship sails straight from India, so these passengers cannot meet it. The rule names no one. I am only applying it as written, and I will not let them land.
audio/g8/clock/donald-smith-one-of-our-d: Donald Smith, one of our directors, lifts the hammer and drives the spike. The photographer asks us all to stand close and keep still. I am very proud. This is the picture the country will remember.
audio/g8/clock/for-two-months-they-hold-: For two months they hold us on board, within sight of the city. Our food and water run short. People here, our own South Asian community, raise money for us and take our case to court.
audio/g8/clock/i-am-an-immigration-offic: I am an immigration officer at the port of Vancouver. On May 23, 1914 a ship called the Komagata Maru comes into the harbour with 376 passengers from Punjab. I have my orders.
audio/g8/clock/i-am-told-they-are-britis: I am told they are British subjects too. But many people in this city want them turned away, and want Canada kept for people like themselves. They tell me so loudly. I do not make the law.
audio/g8/clock/i-came-from-guangdong-in-: I came from Guangdong, in southern China, to build this railway. The company gave men like me the most dangerous work, handling the explosives that blast tunnels and ledges out of the mountain.
audio/g8/clock/i-came-north-from-califor: I came north from California this spring with a pan and a shovel. All winter I heard the same news: there is gold in the sandbars of the Fraser River! Thousands of us rushed here within months, about 30,000 men.
audio/g8/clock/i-know-that-thousands-of-: I know that thousands of men built these miles through the mountains, and that most of them are not standing here. Today I think only of the country that is now joined together.
audio/g8/clock/i-rode-a-steamboat-up-the: I rode a steamboat up the river, then walked. I scoop gravel into my pan, swirl the water, and the heavy yellow flakes settle at the bottom. That is l'or, gold. One good strike and I could buy a farm.
audio/g8/clock/i-sailed-on-the-komagata-: I sailed on the Komagata Maru from Punjab. Most of us are Sikhs, with Muslims and Hindus too. We are British subjects, like people in Canada, and many of us served in the British army.
audio/g8/clock/i-was-paid-about-one-doll: I was paid about one dollar a day, half of what white workers were paid, and I bought my own food and gear out of it. Many men died in rock slides, in blasts, in accidents and from sickness.
audio/g8/clock/it-is-november-7-1885-at-: It is November 7, 1885, at Kray-gell-uh-kee, in Eagle Pass. I am a company man, and I stand in the front row. Today the last spike goes in, and the railway runs from sea to sea.
audio/g8/clock/my-family-has-fished-from: My family has fished from these rocks since long before my grandmother's grandmother. Each fishing rock belongs to a family, and we look after it. Then the miners came, thousands of them, in only a few months.
audio/g8/clock/on-july-23-1914-they-forc: On July 23, 1914 they force us to sail away, with a navy ship's guns pointed at us. Only about 20 of us, who had lived in Canada before, are ever allowed ashore.
audio/g8/clock/that-summer-there-was-fig: That summer there was fighting in the canyon. People on both sides were killed, and villages were burned. It is called the Fraser Canyon War. In the end our leaders made a peace. We are still here, and so is the river.
audio/g8/clock/the-company-did-not-pay-o: The company did not pay our fare home, as many of us had hoped. And this same year, 1885, Canada made a head tax of 50 dollars on every Chinese person coming in. Now I cannot bring my wife and children.
audio/g8/clock/they-dug-up-the-gravel-ba: They dug up the gravel bars where we fish and dry salmon. They took over village sites and fishing rocks. They did not ask us, and we had never agreed to share the river this way.
audio/g8/clock/to-me-the-bank-looked-emp: To me the bank looked empty and free for the taking. I did not stop to ask whose it was.
audio/g8/clock/today-they-drive-the-last: Today they drive the last spike. I am not in the photograph. No Chinese worker is.
audio/g6/s/after-europeans-settled-the-c: After Europeans settled the coasts, the Bee-oth-uck were cut off from the sea they fished. Settlers killed Bee-oth-uck people, and hunger and new sicknesses came. Their numbers fell and fell.
audio/g6/s/but-this-island-was-not-empty: But this island was not empty. The Bee-oth-uck lived across it for a very long time. You say it bee-oth-uck.
audio/g6/s/cape-spear-this-is-the-very-e: Cape Spear! This is the very edge of the map. It is the most easterly point in Canada, and the sun rises here before anywhere else in the country. There is no more east to go.
audio/g6/s/many-settle-at-a-place-called: Many settle at a place called Birchtown. Many waited years for land that never came. Others got less than they were promised, and poorer land too.
audio/g6/s/see-the-cone-shaped-homes-eac: See the cone-shaped homes? Each one is a wee-goo-um. You say it wee-goo-um. It is made of poles covered with birchbark. And look at the canoes. Their sides rise in the middle, to keep out ocean waves.
audio/g6/s/shaw-nuh-dith-it-the-last-kno: Shaw-nuh-dith-it, the last known Bee-oth-uck, died in St. John's in 1829. Before she died she drew maps and pictures, so that her people's story would not be lost.
audio/g6/s/the-acadians-farmed-the-salt-: The Acadians farmed the salt marshes, which mostly left the Meeg-maw hunting grounds alone. How long does a dyke take?
audio/g6/s/the-meeg-mah-call-this-island: The Meeg-mah call this island Oona mahgee. You say Meeg-mah like meeg-mah, and Oona mahgee like oona mahgee.
audio/g6/s/the-soldiers-order-the-acadia: The soldiers order the Acadians to leave their homes. Families are put on ships, and many are split up. The soldiers burn the houses and barns so that nobody can come back.
audio/g6/s/these-long-farms-were-laid-ou: These long farms were laid out along riverbanks that were already the homelands of First Nations. They have lived, fished and travelled along this river for thousands of years, and they still do.
audio/g6/s/they-built-their-homes-and-co: They built their homes and communities anyway. But they were not treated fairly, and in 1792 about 1,200 Black Loyalists left Nova Scotia and sailed to Sierra Leone, in Africa. Many others stayed, and their families are here today.
audio/g6/s/this-is-called-the-deportatio: This is called the Deportation, or le Grand Dérangement. Thousands of Acadians died of sickness and shipwreck on the way.
audio/g6/s/when-it-flies-off-sadie-waves: When it flies off, Sadie waves and says nuh-mool-tess. You say it nuh-mool-tess. It means see you again. I said it too, in case the eagle was listening.
audio/g6/s/when-we-reach-the-shore-again: When we reach the shore again, Sadie says weh-lahl-in. You say it weh-lahl-in. It means thank you. I say it right back, for the paddling lesson.
audio/g7/clock/i-am-a-nakohda-grandmothe: I am a Nakohda grandmother of the plains. I remember when the ground shook with the herds, and the whole camp was fed. In my own lifetime I have watched them vanish. First the herds were smaller. Then they were gone.
audio/g7/s/a-boy-is-waiting-by-a-fence-p: A boy is waiting by a fence post. This is Tyson. He is Nakohda, also called Uh-sin-ih-boyn, and he lives in southern Saskatchewan. His people have lived on these plains for a very long time.
audio/g7/s/ahead-is-the-biggest-lake-of-: Ahead is the biggest lake of them all, Lake Superior. On its northwest shore a river called the Kam-in-iss-tih-kwah runs into it, and the city of Thunder Bay sits beside the water.
audio/g7/s/anish-in-ah-bay-families-buil: Anish-in-ah-bay families built the birchbark canoes, a canoe is un canot. They supplied food such as wild rice and maple sugar, and they guided the brigades. They also trapped furs and traded them.
audio/g7/s/back-on-the-wharf-the-lake-is: Back on the wharf, the lake is turning gold. Zoe says mee-gwetch, which is thank you in Anishinahbay-mowin, the Anish-in-ah-bay language. I say it back. Mine comes out like a sneeze.
audio/g7/s/first-nations-peoples-met-her: First Nations peoples met here to trade, fish and make agreements, among them the ancestors of the Cree, the Anish-in-ah-bay, the Nakohda and the Dakota. Goods travelled huge distances on the rivers.
audio/g7/s/it-grew-from-the-families-of-: It grew from the families of First Nations women (often Cree and Anish-in-ah-bay) and French and Scottish fur traders. Then, over generations, May-tee families married one another and became a new people, a nation.
audio/g7/s/it-is-also-the-territory-of-t: It is also the territory of the neighbouring Treaty 7 nations, the Soo-tih-nah and the Stoney Nakohda. It is a homeland of the May-tee too. They live in Alberta today.
audio/g7/s/this-is-the-alberta-badlands-: This is the Alberta badlands, beside the Red Deer River near the town of Drumheller. It is the traditional territory of the Blackfoot, the Neetsee tahpee. You say it neetsee tahpee.
audio/g7/s/treaty-6-was-made-in-1876-and: Treaty 6 was made in 1876 and Treaty 7 in 1877, between the Crown and the Cree, Nakohda, Blackfoot and other nations. The First Nations understood they were agreeing to share the land.
audio/g7/s/tyson-says-many-nations-call-: Tyson says many nations call the plains home. They are the Nay-hee-yuh-wuk (Plains Cree), the Nakohda, the Neetsee tahpee (Blackfoot), the Dakota and Lakota, and the Soh-toh.
audio/g7/s/you-say-anish-in-ah-bay-like-: You say Anish-in-ah-bay like this: anish-in-ah-bay.
audio/g7/s/you-say-mee-gwetch-like-this-: You say mee-gwetch like this: mee-gwetch. You say Anishinahbay-mowin like this: anishinahbay-mowin.
audio/g7/s/you-say-nakohda-like-this-nak: You say Nakohda like this: nakohda.
audio/g7/s/you-say-nay-hee-yuh-wuk-like-: You say Nay-hee-yuh-wuk like this: nay-hee-yuh-wuk. Neetsee tahpee is neetsee tahpee. Soh-toh is soh-toh.
audio/g7/s/zoe-tells-me-the-ojibwe-one-o: Zoe tells me the Ojibwe, one of the Anish-in-ah-bay nations, have lived around this lake since long before there was any fort. Fort William First Nation is right beside the city today.
